I don't mean to be dramatic — ok, maybe a little — but there's a lot of AI apocalypse talk these days.

An Anthropic researcher's resignation and warning earlier this week that AI giants are "gambling with our lives" sparked a wider conversation. Mainly: Is AI actually going to kill us all?

The debate quickly broke into the mainstream, with billionaire hedge fund investor Paul Tudor Jones calling AI a "Category 6 hurricane." Even my 71-year-old mom texted me about whether this was "truth or hysteria."

Let's start with the basics: Can AI really wipe us out? And if so, how would it do it?

BI's Thibault Spirlet posed those questions to senior AI researchers. They outlined short-term risks, like AI fueling human attacks, and wider concerns as we cede more control to AI.

Hollywood has also spent decades imagining how it would all go down.

As for the odds of all this happening, that's a mixed bag. One notable mention is Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI," who said there's a 10% chance AI wipes out humanity in a decade. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher, also spoke to BI about why "AI is not loyal to us."

But why not go straight to the source? We decided to ask AI how it would go about destroying humanity. It turns we'll ultimately be the ones to blame.

Not everyone is taking such a somber view.

The internet is poking fun at some of the alarmist language.

AI companies have made a habit of talking out of both sides of their mouths. Warnings about the tech's "threats" also help them market the power of their products and the important role they play.

That doesn't mean there isn't cause for concern. Many in the AI community have acknowledged they can't slow down even if they wanted to. Losing ground to rivals, or China, isn't an option with so much money at stake.

That still doesn't mean we're on the cusp of something terrible. Fear sells. And dramatic, high-stakes storylines pitched to investors reinforce the idea that these companies are on the frontlines of a revolution, and worth the high price tag.

Because if people stop buying the AI hype, that could pose a real problem for a stock market basically built on it. Fitch Ratings already warned an AI bubble bursting would have a wide-reaching impact.

So AI could take us all down, just not how you think.

items.title: Could AI really kill off humanity within the decade? Expert Q&A
items.summary: Samuel Boivin Artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity this decade, according to three researchers from the US company Anthropic . One of the employees, Jacob Coxon, has quit the AI firm. His predictions were backed by two other current Anthropic researchers in posts on social media. On X, Coxon claimed: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.” It’s not the first time AI researchers and companies have issued such assessments. Here, Kate Devlin, professor of artificial intelligence & society, explains what is behind them and whether there’s anything different about the latest warning. The latest claims about AI have come from a researcher who resigned from Anthropic. What is your general view on what has happened here? To give this a sense of perspective, we should remember that it’s one AI company ex-employee posting on a platform known for grandiose claims, which was then quoted by a current AI company employee who put a figure on the risk of human extinction at greater than 10%. So, it’s another doom-laden narrative about the supposed threat from AI. There is some dialling back from this in a follow up tweet from current Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger that read : “I think the risk from present models is low. What I’m worried about is superintelligence”. These tweets have gained huge coverage because these kinds of things always do. It taps into our very primal fears – and our decades of watching dystopian sci-fi. The claims from Jacob Coxon were backed by current employees of Anthropic. Why do you think AI companies are happy to support these kinds of claims in public? It’s likely that these men believe what they’re saying, but we’ve heard warnings like this for years. It does seem odd that AI companies are okay with these kinds of claims. Let’s remember that they are constantly looking for investment and, in return, they promise the most powerful and dominant models. What could be more powerful than a model that threatens our very existence? One theory for doom-mongering by AI companies is that they want to avoid regulation. Do you think outside regulation of AI companies is inevitable? It has been incredibly difficult to regulate AI, certainly at an international level. There has been little appetite for AI to be regulated in the US because there’s a view that regulation might stifle innovation. The UK doesn’t have any AI-specific laws either, just existing laws that might apply in some cases. China began to introduce national-level laws but has now replaced that with technical standards and sector regulation. The EU remains the only place where there is dedicated AI regulation . However, it looks like this has kicked off yet another call for better regulation, and we’re seeing that at present in US Congress and in the Houses of Parliament in the UK. There is another angle, in that industry might be on board with regulation, as big tech companies would have the money to comply, but it could knock out their competitors with smaller budgets, so it would leave the leaders in dominant positions. How far away are we from the kind of superintelligent AI mentioned in the latest warnings? We don’t have superintelligence . I’m reluctant to put a time frame on that. Often people say “5-10 years” but that’s happened a lot in AI and 5-10 years pass without anything arising. It also depends on what is meant by superintelligence. Something that is conscious and thinks for itself? That might never happen. In this case, it doesn’t really matter, as there are other harms already happening from AI, and there are other ways things can go wrong, though probably not at the existential level that’s being suggested here. For example, AI is energy-hungry. It needs water to cool data centres. It has a damaging environmental impact. There are also issues around the content generated by AI, anything from a lack of plurality in the models’ outputs (meaning that the information it returns is homogenised, converging on particular viewpoints) to the spread of misinformation and disinformation. We also know there is hidden labour in the AI supply chain: there are people working in terrible conditions to deliver the technology. And we know that it’s having an impact on people’s lives in terms of how it’s changing the workplace . What are the potential practical ways in which AI could actually wipe out humans? “Wiping out” is a bit extreme but there are some dangerous threats. There are the “bad actor” scenarios where AI is used destructively, like creating weapons or deadly viruses. More mundane, but potentially very destructive, are AI agents let loose due to human carelessness or incompetence, hacking or taking control of insecure systems. A survey we recently ran at King’s College London found that the UK public are feeling increasingly negative about AI, and that 42% of people are deliberately limiting their AI use . With claims from tech companies that it poses a direct threat to our existence, it will be unsurprising if public opinion dips even further. Kate Devlin does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

items.title: SpaceX has struck a $1 billion a month compute deal with a mystery customer
items.summary: SpaceX is targeting $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year. Spencer Platt/Getty Images SpaceX has closed yet another AI compute deal with a mystery customer. The agreement is worth over $1 billion a month, SpaceX's CFO said on Thursday. It follows similar deals with Anthropic and Google as Elon Musk's rocket company cashes in on its Colossus data centers. SpaceX is cashing in on the surging demand for AI compute. CFO Bret Johnsen told a Goldman Sachs conference on Thursday that SpaceX had clinched another major data center deal worth over $1 billion a month. "Just earlier this month, we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year," Johnsen said. Johnsen did not say who the customer was, but added that the deal gave him "even more conviction" that SpaceX would hit its target of $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year. The latest deal adds to agreements SpaceX has struck with Google and Anthropic to rent out capacity in its massive Colossus data centers in Mississippi and Tennessee. Anthropic agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion a month through to May 2029 as it battled to meet growing demand for its Claude AI model, while the deal Google, which is a major SpaceX shareholder, agreed in June is worth $920 million a month . Securing compute to run and train the most powerful AI models has become a huge bottleneck for AI companies, with the likes of OpenAI and Meta embarking on multibillion-dollar data center building sprees that have sparked significant public backlash. The race to gain access to cutting-edge GPUs and data centers has turned into a major revenue opportunity for SpaceX, which acquired a significant amount of unused data center capacity when it merged with Musk's AI startup xAI in February. Johnsen told investors in the company's Q2 earnings last month that SpaceX had already signed $6.7 billion in cloud services revenue in the first few weeks of the third quarter. The influx of revenue comes as SpaceX continues to burn eye-watering amounts of money on building new AI infrastructure. The rocket company spent $16 billion on AI infrastructure in the second quarter of 2026, with executives telling investors to expect similar levels of spending for the rest of the year. If everything goes to plan, a lot of that infrastructure will end up in space. Elon Musk has bet that the solution to the public backlash and energy crunch data centers are facing on Earth lies in building a network of AI satellites, and SpaceX is planning to launch its first orbital data centers at the end of next year. SpaceX is targeting $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year.

Spencer Platt/Getty Images

  • SpaceX has closed yet another AI compute deal with a mystery customer.
  • The agreement is worth over $1 billion a month, SpaceX's CFO said on Thursday.
  • It follows similar deals with Anthropic and Google as Elon Musk's rocket company cashes in on its Colossus data centers.

SpaceX is cashing in on the surging demand for AI compute.

CFO Bret Johnsen told a Goldman Sachs conference on Thursday that SpaceX had clinched another major data center deal worth over $1 billion a month.

"Just earlier this month, we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year," Johnsen said.

Johnsen did not say who the customer was, but added that the deal gave him "even more conviction" that SpaceX would hit its target of $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year.

The latest deal adds to agreements SpaceX has struck with Google and Anthropic to rent out capacity in its massive Colossus data centers in Mississippi and Tennessee.

Anthropic agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion a month through to May 2029 as it battled to meet growing demand for its Claude AI model, while the deal Google, which is a major SpaceX shareholder, agreed in June is worth $920 million a month.

Securing compute to run and train the most powerful AI models has become a huge bottleneck for AI companies, with the likes of OpenAI and Meta embarking on multibillion-dollar data center building sprees that have sparked significant public backlash.

The race to gain access to cutting-edge GPUs and data centers has turned into a major revenue opportunity for SpaceX, which acquired a significant amount of unused data center capacity when it merged with Musk's AI startup xAI in February.

Johnsen told investors in the company's Q2 earnings last month that SpaceX had already signed $6.7 billion in cloud services revenue in the first few weeks of the third quarter.

The influx of revenue comes as SpaceX continues to burn eye-watering amounts of money on building new AI infrastructure.

The rocket company spent $16 billion on AI infrastructure in the second quarter of 2026, with executives telling investors to expect similar levels of spending for the rest of the year.

If everything goes to plan, a lot of that infrastructure will end up in space.

Elon Musk has bet that the solution to the public backlash and energy crunch data centers are facing on Earth lies in building a network of AI satellites, and SpaceX is planning to launch its first orbital data centers at the end of next year.

items.title: Trump snapped at a reporter after a question about his $5,000 promise to voters: 'You're the worst'
items.summary: President Donald Trump speaks to reporters on the tarmac before boarding Air Force One after attending the Republican Midterm Convention. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images A reporter asked Trump why he needed to give voters $5,000 if his economic policies were working. It didn't go well. He blamed Biden, and leaned forward and glared at her when she tried a follow-up question. A reporter asked President Donald Trump why he needed to incentivize voters with a $5,000 check if his economic policies were working, and it seemed to strike a nerve. On Wednesday, Trump told the Republican Party's midterm convention that every US citizen would receive a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November's midterms. The proposal could cost upward of $1.3 trillion if every US citizen received the payment, though Vice President JD Vance later said wealthy people would be excluded. Joe Lonsdale, the cofounder of Palantir , was among the critics of the pledge and said the payment would be akin to a "bribe." When a reporter questioned Trump about the proposal on the airport tarmac in Dallas on Thursday night, the president appeared to snap. After noting that the US has $40 trillion in debt, the reporter asked: "If your economic policies are working, why do you need an incentive for people to turn out and vote?" Trump responded: "I didn't do it for turning out the vote. I'm doing it as a reward for people having to put up with five years, and four years, of a horrible, horrible situation caused by Biden." He repeated the point, calling the promised dividend "almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden's policies." Q: On the checks, we have $40 trillion in debt. If your economic policies are working, why do you need an incentive for people to turn out to vote? TRUMP: I'm doing it as a reward for people having to put up for five years and four years of a horrible situation caused by Biden… pic.twitter.com/Iq4LpS1pNt — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 11, 2026 As the reporter began a follow-up question, Trump said "not you," while pointing to another journalist. The reporter continued: "You also offered checks during… tariff refunds checks, and that didn't happen, Mr. President." This was a reference to Trump's November 2025 pledge to send $2,000 tariff-rebate checks, which have not been paid out. He also floated "DOGE dividends" in early 2025, which would have provided Americans with a one-time check of up to $5,000. They also never materialized. Trump interrupted with another "not you," then leaned toward her, glared, and repeated it for a third time. "Your network and you, you're the worst," he said. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The Only 2 Moats That Actually Work In The AI Era
items.summary: By SC Moatti If your pitch still leads with “we use AI,” you’re describing infrastructure, not a business. Consider that 97% of the products nominated for this year’s Products That Count Product Awards are deeply integrated with AI, highlighting the extent to which the days of AI as a differentiator are officially gone. SC Moatti, founding managing partner of Mighty Capital. The real moat investors are seeking today is something many founders cannot identify: What will survive a well-funded competitor who could launch tomorrow with a better model. We analyzed Crunchbase data on 576 venture-backed, AI B2B companies that raised $50 million-plus rounds since the start of 2025 using Hamilton Helmer’s 7 Powers framework and layered in insights from Products That Count’s 600,000-plus product leader community. The data gives a clear answer: When building is nearly free, the only moats that hold are those that a model cannot generate. Two of them work without requiring you to out-raise OpenAI . Two of them are traps. And one isn’t a game most founders are playing. Counter-positioning: The moat that costs nothing to defend Counter-positioning is what happens when a newcomer builds a business model so structurally different that the incumbent can’t copy it without destroying their own economics. Netflix versus Blockbuster is the canonical example. Blockbuster could have matched the subscription model, but doing so would have gutted late-fee revenue, which kept their stores alive. So they didn’t, until it was too late. In the AI era, this power is rare and underutilized. Only 5% of companies in our dataset leverage counter-positioning. Investors price that scarcity at a median enterprise value of 5.3x per dollar raised — the highest multiple of any power in the analysis. The pattern shows up in vertically integrated AI insurers that sell directly to employers, a model traditional brokers can’t replicate without cannibalizing their own relationships and underwriting margins. It shows up in AI-native revenue management systems that would gut the high-margin consulting revenue legacy vendors depend on if those vendors tried to match them. The incumbent sees the threat. They choose not to respond. That rational inaction is the moat. For founders, the diagnostic question is this: Could a well-resourced incumbent copy your model if they wanted to? The right signal is answering “technically yes, but it would cost them more than it would cost us to build.” Network economies: The moat that builds itself Network economies arise when a product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join. At scale, this tends toward winner-take-all outcomes within the network’s boundaries, whether in geography, professional context or industry vertical. LinkedIn is the textbook case: More recruiters attract more candidates, which in turn attract more professionals, which in turn attract more recruiters. In our dataset, network economies appear in only 5% of companies, but command a 4.2x multiple. That makes it the most capital-efficient path to a strong valuation premium available to founders today. The B2B variant here is particularly underappreciated. Rather than individual users as nodes, the network connects companies: brands to factories, advertisers to audiences, platforms to partners. Every new participant makes the network more valuable for every existing participant. The data that accumulates across those interactions — costing, production cycles, audience behavior — compounds in ways that become progressively harder to replicate. Getting both sides of a two-sided market to commit simultaneously is hard. But founders who solve the cold-start problem own something that a well-funded competitor with a better model still cannot buy. What looks like a moat but isn’t? At 44%, cornered resources like proprietary data, unique IP and exclusive access command the second-highest prevalence in our dataset. But they also have the worst multiple: 2.6x. Because investors have watched too many proprietary datasets get eroded by foundation models and synthetic data, if a data advantage doesn’t compound in ways that get harder to replicate over time, it can’t be considered a moat. Switching costs are the most crowded power at 37%, and look like a moat because customers really don’t leave. But the cost of building them creates a problem, because the requirement for deep enterprise entanglement — baked-in instrumentation, institutional memory, rearchitecture risk — means expensive sales cycles before the stickiness kicks in. The multiple is comparable to network economies (4x), but the capital required to reach it is roughly 10x higher. It’s a viable path for founders who build a product-led growth motion to reduce that cost, or who engineer a reason for users to collaborate on the platform, converting switching costs into network economies over time. Scale economies are not the game most founders are playing. The median multiple, excluding OpenAI and Anthropic , collapses from 6.1x to 3.2x, and 88% of the category’s capital belongs to those two companies. Believing your unit economics improve with growth does not equate to building a scale moat. The gap between the two is measured in billions of dollars that most startups will never raise. The only question that matters Every company in this dataset has AI in its product. The ones commanding premium multiples have built something underneath the AI that a model cannot generate on its own. That something is structural. It lies in the business model design or the network architecture, rather than model quality, feature set or data volume. It answers the question every founder should be able to state in one sentence: What about my business would survive a competitor who starts today with more capital and a better model? If you can’t answer that question, you’re building a product. The founders commanding 4x to 5x multiples are building a power. SC Moatti is the founding managing partner of Mighty Capital and board chair at Products That Count . As a venture capitalist honored on the Kauffman Top 30 Index and Power100, she invested in pioneering companies including Amplitude , Netskope and Groq . She earned a reputation for developing products that people love during the cloud and mobile era, when she built products that billions of people use at Meta and Siebel Systems , won industry awards and nominations from The Wall Street Journal and the Emmy’s Foundation , and wrote an award-winning bestseller on what makes a great product. She holds a master’s in electrical engineering and a Stanford MBA, and is a Kauffman Fellow and member of Young Presidents Organization . Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: How This Doctor-Turned-Startup-Founder Decided To Fix The Healthcare Staffing Crunch: Make Employers Apply
items.summary: Editor’s note: The following is the sixth profile in a series of articles about startup founders from non-technical backgrounds who have launched successful venture-backed companies. Read the previous interviews with MagicSchool AI founder Adeel Khan here , Trunk Tools founder Sarah Buchner here , Tabs founder Ali Hussain here , Craft founder Ilya Levtov here , and GC AI founder Cecilia Ziniti here . After completing medical school in London, Iman Abuzeid decided not to pursue a residency. Her father was disappointed. But she didn’t change her mind because she lost interest in healthcare. Instead, Abuzeid realized she wanted to work on problems affecting more people than she could treat individually. Iman Abuzeid, co-founder and CEO of Incredible Health. (Courtesy photo) “Working as a doctor is great, but you’re only working with one patient at a time,” she said in an interview with Crunchbase News. With software, “you have millions of users using your products.” Abuzeid went on to co-found Incredible Health , a San Francisco-based healthcare hiring platform that has raised about $97.5 million from investors such as Andreessen Horowitz , Base10 Partners , Obvious Ventures , Precursor Ventures and NFX . It says its products are used by 1.5 million healthcare professionals — including 1 in 2 U.S. nurses — and 1,500 healthcare employers. Before launching Incredible Health in 2017, Abuzeid trained as a doctor, advised healthcare companies at Booz Allen and McKinsey , and worked as a product manager at a health tech startup, but didn’t know how to code software. An M.D. who chose not to practice Originally from Sudan, Abuzeid was born and raised in Saudi Arabia and also lived in the United Arab Emirates. She moved to London at 18, where she completed her undergraduate education and medical school. Her interest in business predated her medical career. Both of her grandfathers were entrepreneurs in Sudan, and she grew up hearing about the companies they built. By medical school, she was increasingly drawn to the reach that entrepreneurship and technology could offer. After earning her medical degree, Abuzeid immigrated to New York at age 24. Her time in healthcare consulting at Booz Allen and McKinsey exposed her to the strategy, operations and economics behind the healthcare system, she said. She later earned an MBA from the Wharton School, specializing in healthcare and entrepreneurship, and moved to San Francisco in 2013. There, she joined an early-stage healthcare technology company as a product manager. The role taught her how to work with engineers, data scientists and designers, as well as how software products are built and grown. It was also where she met Rome Portlock , the software engineer who would become her co-founder at Incredible Health. Abuzeid still does not code, although she has experimented with newer AI-assisted coding tools. Portlock, an MIT -trained engineer who she calls “the best engineer I’ve ever worked with,” has led Incredible Health’s engineering and data teams from the beginning. But Abuzeid, the startup’s CEO, argues that a software founder’s central job isn’t writing code. “At the end of the day, when it comes to creating software companies, it’s about solving problems,” she said. “It’s about identifying the markets, understanding the problems customers are facing and figuring out ways to solve them.” A mismatch in healthcare hiring The problem behind Incredible Health surfaced through conversations the founders were having with people they knew. Doctors in Abuzeid’s family and circle of friends frequently complained about understaffing. At the same time, nurses in Portlock’s family described applying to numerous jobs and often receiving no response. The two accounts did not line up. Healthcare is the largest U.S. labor sector by number of workers, Abuzeid said, and it faces severe staffing shortages. Yet experienced nurses were struggling to get the attention of employers that urgently needed them. “We started to dig into it more, and we were like, ‘This doesn’t make any sense,’” she recalls. The founders discovered that hospital recruiting teams were often small, overwhelmed by applicant volume, and reliant on manual processes. Incredible Health’s marketplace reverses the usual hiring process so that employers are actually the ones applying to healthcare workers. The software automates screening and matching for permanent jobs at hospitals, surgery centers, home health organizations and other healthcare facilities. The service is free for healthcare professionals. Employers pay an annual subscription to use the marketplace and the company’s other hiring software. Customers include Kaiser Permanente , Tenet Health , Trinity Health , NewYork-Presbyterian and Johns Hopkins . A selective approach to fundraising Incredible Health has raised approximately $97 million across seed, Series A and Series B rounds. It was a process, she admits. She spoke with about 70 investors while raising the company’s seed round. Eight invested, including Obvious Ventures and Precursor Ventures . At that stage, Abuzeid said, she had to educate investors about the healthcare labor market and persuade them that she and Portlock were the right founders to address it. “I think it was the vision and the mission and the team,” she said. “At that point, you’re really investing in the founders.” Each of Incredible Health’s funding rounds was oversubscribed, Abuzeid said. She attributes that partly to raising from a position of financial strength. The company generally operates close to cash-flow break-even and at times has been cash-flow positive. Overall, Abuzeid said she is selective about which investors she approaches. Specifically, she prefers firms with marketplace experience and partners who have previously operated companies. She also prioritizes investors who have already backed women or founders of color. “I don’t want to be the first,” she said. “I’m not here to overcome someone’s bias. That’s not a good use of my time.” While she acknowledges structural disparities in venture funding, Abuzeid said she didn’t choose to work with Portlock because she believed she needed a male co-founder. Rather, she recognized that a strong technical partner would balance her own skills and abilities. Overall, Abuzeid believes female founders generally need to emphasize ambition. In her view, investors are used to hearing expansive visions from male founders, and women should be equally vocal about the size of the companies they intend to build. “It’s really important to be ambitious and to be very clear about your vision and what you’re trying to achieve,” she said. Automating the first interview In 2025, like many other startups, Incredible Health incorporated AI into its product lineup. The company developed the agents with healthcare systems including Baylor Scott & White Health , Sutter Health , NewYork-Presbyterian, Johns Hopkins and Tenet H ealth . Working with customers during the development process made it easier for Incredible Health to incorporate the technology into established enterprise workflows, Abuzeid noted. One agent, Lyn, conducts the initial recruiter interview, asks clinical and behavioral questions, explains an employer’s value proposition, and discusses available roles. It then hands the candidate off for a possible interview with a hiring manager. A second agent, Gail, helps healthcare professionals create résumés and practice for interviews. Abuzeid said Lyn has reduced hiring time by 30%. Three-quarters of interviews now occur within 24 hours of a candidate applying, compared with up to two weeks previously. About 40% take place at night or on weekends, when recruiters are less likely to be available. The AI products clearly extend Incredible Health’s initial mission of removing hiring delays in the healthcare industry. They also reflect the founders’ complementary roles. Portlock continues to oversee engineering, data and technical architecture, while Abuzeid’s work draws on her experience across medicine, healthcare consulting and product management. For Abuzeid, that distinction shows why she does not consider technical chops a prerequisite for founding a software company. “At the end of the day, when it comes to creating software companies,” she said, “it’s about solving problems.” Related Crunchbase queries: Global Venture Funding To AI Healthcare Companies In 2026 Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026 Related reading: ‘Nobody Wanted to Give A Former Principal Money’: How An Educator Built An Edtech AI Startup With $63M From VCs How A Teenage Carpenter Became The Founder Of AI Construction Startup Trunk Tools From Humanities To AI: How Ali Hussain Built Fintech Tabs Into A $400M Startup Craft’s Ilya Levtov Never Learned To Code. He Built A Software Company Anyway. A Startup General Counsel Knew What Corporate Lawyers Needed From AI. So She Built It. Illustration: Dom Guzman

The service is free for healthcare professionals. Employers pay an annual subscription to use the marketplace and the company’s other hiring software. Customers include Kaiser Permanente, Tenet Health, Trinity Health, NewYork-Presbyterian and Johns Hopkins.

A selective approach to fundraising

Incredible Health has raised approximately $97 million across seed, Series A and Series B rounds.

It was a process, she admits. She spoke with about 70 investors while raising the company’s seed round. Eight invested, including Obvious Ventures and Precursor Ventures.

At that stage, Abuzeid said, she had to educate investors about the healthcare labor market and persuade them that she and Portlock were the right founders to address it.

“I think it was the vision and the mission and the team,” she said. “At that point, you’re really investing in the founders.”

Each of Incredible Health’s funding rounds was oversubscribed, Abuzeid said. She attributes that partly to raising from a position of financial strength. The company generally operates close to cash-flow break-even and at times has been cash-flow positive.

Overall, Abuzeid said she is selective about which investors she approaches. Specifically, she prefers firms with marketplace experience and partners who have previously operated companies. She also prioritizes investors who have already backed women or founders of color.

“I don’t want to be the first,” she said. “I’m not here to overcome someone’s bias. That’s not a good use of my time.”

While she acknowledges structural disparities in venture funding, Abuzeid said she didn’t choose to work with Portlock because she believed she needed a male co-founder. Rather, she recognized that a strong technical partner would balance her own skills and abilities.

Overall, Abuzeid believes female founders generally need to emphasize ambition. In her view, investors are used to hearing expansive visions from male founders, and women should be equally vocal about the size of the companies they intend to build.

“It’s really important to be ambitious and to be very clear about your vision and what you’re trying to achieve,” she said.

Automating the first interview

In 2025, like many other startups, Incredible Health incorporated AI into its product lineup.

The company developed the agents with healthcare systems including Baylor Scott & White Health, Sutter Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, Johns Hopkins and Tenet Health. Working with customers during the development process made it easier for Incredible Health to incorporate the technology into established enterprise workflows, Abuzeid noted.

One agent, Lyn, conducts the initial recruiter interview, asks clinical and behavioral questions, explains an employer’s value proposition, and discusses available roles. It then hands the candidate off for a possible interview with a hiring manager.

A second agent, Gail, helps healthcare professionals create résumés and practice for interviews.

Abuzeid said Lyn has reduced hiring time by 30%. Three-quarters of interviews now occur within 24 hours of a candidate applying, compared with up to two weeks previously. About 40% take place at night or on weekends, when recruiters are less likely to be available.

The AI products clearly extend Incredible Health’s initial mission of removing hiring delays in the healthcare industry. They also reflect the founders’ complementary roles. Portlock continues to oversee engineering, data and technical architecture, while Abuzeid’s work draws on her experience across medicine, healthcare consulting and product management.

For Abuzeid, that distinction shows why she does not consider technical chops a prerequisite for founding a software company.

“At the end of the day, when it comes to creating software companies,” she said, “it’s about solving problems.”

items.title: Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriously | Gaby Hinsliff
items.summary: AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late Another day, another horseman of the apocalypse galloping over the horizon. Lately we have heard from so many AI doomers – tech whistleblowers popping up to warn that their work is probably going to kill us – that we’re becoming almost blase about it. Humanity wiped out within a decade? Well, only if another world war or the climate crisis doesn’t get us first. Since it’s never clear whether the tech threat is real, or just a twisted form of hype from an industry that drums up investment by making their products sound more powerful than they really are, most of us settle for trying not to think about it too hard. But something about the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s very public resignation from the cutting-edge American lab Anthropic, via a post on X arguing that he can’t keep working for companies “gambling with our lives”, has cut through where bigger names have not. Most chillingly, he claimed that colleagues still at Anthropic aren’t staying because they think he’s wrong about the dangers of pursuing self-improving super intelligence – the holy grail of machines that are not just smarter than humans but capable of building their own even more powerful successors, evolving independently of humans – but because they’re afraid of ceding the field to people with fewer scruples. His colleagues, Coxon said, talk routinely about the “endgame” or the “ crunch time ”, meaning that what they do in the next year or two will decide the fate of humanity. Whether that’s true or simply self-aggrandising techbro delusion, what he describes is an industry now practically begging to be saved from itself. Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

items.title: 4 tricks to ace a job interview, according to a deception and human behavior expert
items.summary: Pamela Meyer said that people should religiously ask themselves if what they're saying advances the conversation. Pamela Meyer Pamela Meyer is a fraud examiner and human behavior expert who wrote "How to Read the Room." She shares interview power moves, like using the plural pronoun "we," which emphasizes collaboration. Meyer also suggests speaking without filler words and using bold transitions to signal confidence. Acing an interview — like any corporate challenge — often comes down to how well you can read others. Pamela Meyer, the CEO of Calibrate, Inc., trains organizations in fraud detection, insider-threat mitigation, and security awareness. In her new book, "How to Read the Room," she explores how social awareness shapes leadership, negotiations, and decision-making. Learning to read others isn't just a skill for leaders, says Meyer, a certified fraud examiner. It can help candidates make it to the next round of interviews. "Reading the room is, it turns out, a foundational skill," Meyer told Business Insider, adding that it's "entirely teachable." Meyer writes that while job seekers may worry about stumbling over an interview question or forgetting to mention a key accomplishment, interviewers often form personality judgments based largely on nonverbal cues, including eye contact and nodding, rather than what candidates actually say. Here are four interview power moves she recommends for standing out in the interview process: Use the term "we" Meyer said in her book that using plural pronouns, like "we" instead of "I," makes a person seem more collaborative and can make you seem friendlier. In general, Meyer said that candidates should also focus the conversation on how they'd work with the team, not just what they can accomplish on their own. Deflect strategically If the interviewer asks an inappropriate question about family or your personal life, Meyer wrote that candidates should gracefully redirect the conversation by asking another question. Doing so can increase hiring chances and likability more than telling the truth or confronting the interviewer, Meyer said. In general, Meyer told Business Insider that people should "ask themselves religiously: Is what I'm going to say going to advance this conversation?" Many people fall in the trap of talking too much or over-explaining, but just because you're prompted doesn't mean you have to fill the silence or overshare. "Speaking less — and more meaningfully — will give you outsized influence," Meyer said. Avoid filler words Meyer said that speaking clearly and with fewer filler words, such as "um" or "like," signals control rather than uncertainty. That may mean deliberately slowing down your speaking pace when answering questions. She suggests practicing answering prompts out loud and spontaneously, rather than memorizing specific responses. She also advises using bold transitions in interviews like, "What matters more here is… ." Finish strong Meyer said a candidate's initial responses correspond most with the overall success of the interview. However, a strong finish can make up for earlier weakness, she wrote in the book. She said candidates should use the final minutes of the interview to ask thoughtful questions . Demonstrating curiosity is a crucial way to show confidence in an interview, rather than appearing overly excited or nodding your head a lot, she said. "One of the best ways to seem confident is just to ask an interesting question and let it drop," Meyer said, adding that the ideal style of confidence is "more contained, more thoughtful, and it's more curious." "One of the best ways to seem confident is just to ask an interesting question and let it drop," Meyer said, adding that the ideal style of confidence is "more contained, more thoughtful, and it's more curious."

items.title: How to say 'no' at work without hurting your career
items.summary: Saying "no" is a professional skill, according to etiquette experts. Teera Konakan/Getty Images Today's tip to get better at work: The best way to say "no" to more work when you are at capacity. Setting boundaries helps maintain high-quality work and prevents burnout. If you're given a new task when you already have a lot on your plate, ask what you should prioritize. Get better at: Setting boundaries Today's move Don't say '"yes" to more work just because you're asked, especially if your plate is full and you could compromise your other work. If you're given a shorter-term ask and you have another fast-approaching deadline, tell your manager that you'd be happy to take on the additional project but in order to do it well, you'd need to deprioritize something else. Ask them what they would like you to focus on. Why it works Instead of refusing the work, you're communicating your current workload and asking them to verbalize what should be prioritized. This provides your manager with the context they need to decide what's most important, and puts the decision of what gets cut or put on the back burner in their hands. Try it today Write down everything on your to-do list and ask yourself if you'd be able to take on an additional project if you were asked at this moment. If you can't think of how to make room for it, you're probably already at capacity. Try proactively having a conversation with your manager about your workload so that they're aware. The bottom line In the first quarter of 2026, workers mentioned burnout in Glassdoor reviews 2.5 times more often than they did before the pandemic. In the midst of workplace changes, layoffs, and AI changing the pace of work, employees may be defaulting to taking on more. items.title: NYC's best shot at affordable housing has hit some roadblocks
items.summary: Vacant office buildings are one of NYC's main options to boost housing supply. Gary Hershorn/Getty Images Several NYC office-to-apartments conversions faced safety issues this summer. Retrofitting plumbing, windows, and floor plans for housing is costly and complicated. To solve the supply shortage, conversions are here to stay. Office-to-residential conversions — one of New York City's leading housing strategies — have been shaken by recent safety concerns. This summer, a "stop work" order was issued for the former Pfizer building in Midtown due to structural issues with steel columns, prompting fears of a collapse and temporary evacuation of the surrounding area. A lower Manhattan conversion at 222 Broadway was briefly halted over reports of a cracked horizontal concrete beam, and a Midtown East conversion — 750 Third Avenue — was partially stopped, also because of problems with steel columns. Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to build 200,000 new homes during his first term. The issues with the office conversions raise questions about one of NYC's main means of boosting housing supply . Business Insider spoke with policy analysts and developers about the safety concerns, construction challenges, and what it all means for the future. Office conversions require costly retrofitting When constructing dense housing , cities have a few options: They can build from scratch, build above existing businesses, or convert underused hotels and offices into apartments. Offices, in particular, are ripe for housing because many were fully or partially vacated at the height of the pandemic . The NYC office vacancy rate was 15.2% in the second quarter of 2024, the state comptroller reported, up from 7.8% in the second quarter of 2016. Former workspaces provide a lot of space, but developers and policy analysts said construction can be challenging — part of the reason conversions have faced structural safety issues. Offices typically have a different foundation setup than residential buildings. Emma Waters, a senior housing policy analyst at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said this makes it more difficult to adjust floor plans , add floors, and split into units with their own kitchens and bathrooms. Plumbing is a concern. In a hotel conversion, for example, the space is already equipped with the piping and water system needed to sustain hundreds of toilets and showers. Offices might only have one or two bathroom setups per floor, which construction crews need to supplement during the conversion process. Most offices also have large sets of windows along the exterior, without a central courtyard or interior windows. Ensuring every apartment has adequate sunlight — something that is both nice for residents and required by many building codes — can be a logistical challenge. And residential windows must open for fire safety, a feature not built into most office windows. Updating all of that infrastructure takes significant time and resources. "In hotels, every room has natural light," NYC property developer David Schwartz previously told Business Insider. "That's the biggest problem. That's why the office conversions are much more difficult — because once you start cutting out concrete in the middle of a building, you've put yourself into a really complicated project." Waters added that conversions are easier in smaller buildings. "It is very, very project dependent on whether it's going to be faster and more cost-effective than building a new building, or if it's going to be super complex and require a lot of expensive retrofits," she said. She added that co-living models — like having individual bedroom spaces but central, shared kitchens and bathrooms among neighbors — could be a happy medium. Conversions remain important for housing supply Despite elevated safety concerns, office conversions remain one of New York's top housing priorities. Manhattan converted 5 million square feet of office space in 2024, up from 2.7 million the year prior. Aside from a dip during the pandemic, conversions like this have been trending upward. There are also existing tax and subsidy programs that incentivize office-to-housing projects. The state rolled back a 60-year-old restrictive zoning law this year, making it easier to build denser apartment buildings. The Mamdani administration has taken specific actions to streamline permitting and construction, and the newest federal housing bill includes grants to help cities like NYC offset the cost of converting commercial space into homes. All owners and developers for the Manhattan office projects flagged for safety issues have made public statements that they are reviewing safety documentation and protocols for the buildings and making repairs. The developers did not respond with specific comments to Business Insider. At a July press conference about the compromised Midtown building, Mamdani said, "Safety is paramount for us in every decision we are making right now." Meanwhile, market-rate rents in New York City continue to climb, reaching $5,000 a month in Manhattan this summer as supply dwindles. The majority of residents are rent-burdened , meaning they spend at least 30% of their total income on housing. Structural issues may slow down a few specific projects, but Waters said office conversions are here to stay. If Mamdani plans to build 200,000 new homes — and make rent more affordable in the long run — every new building with a few hundred units counts toward that goal. "It's definitely an all of the above, as needed situation," Waters said. "We are really, really deep into this supply deficit. There's not going to be a silver bullet." items.title: Most Olympians don't make millions. This bobsledder rented out his home to boost his income while competing around the world.
items.summary: Boone Niederhofer competed for Team USA in bobsled at the 2026 Winter Olympics. Courtesy of Boone Niederhofer Boone Niederhofer, a former collegiate football player, began his bobsledding career after a COVID-era layoff. Today, he balances a full-time engineering job, Olympic training, and fatherhood. He explains how he created additional income during the Olympic season by renting out his home. Some might assume that making it to the Olympics brings financial security, but for many athletes in lesser-known sports, it's not a windfall. In fact, the costs can be higher than they pay for some Olympians. "Athletes will go into debt trying to chase their dream," Olympian Boone Niederhofer told Business Insider. Equipment, travel, and lodging can add up quickly, while "the realities of life are still there, even for people who make the Olympics." For Niederhofer, a bobsled push athlete and petroleum engineer from Texas, the path to the 2026 Winter Olympics required more than speed and strength. He worked full time, trained around his job, and turned his family's Midland home into a four-month mid-term rental while they traveled through Europe for the World Cup season. The rental income helped make it possible for his wife, Chloe, and their two young kids to join him rather than spend months apart. Before bobsled, Niederhofer played football at Texas A&M. Courtesy of Boone Niederhofer Bobsled, familiar to many Americans mostly through the 1993 movie "Cool Runnings," tends to draw athletes from football and track and field. "Any athlete that is fast and powerful and strong is going to be a good bobsledder," explained Niederhofer, who developed those traits playing football at Texas A&M before an ACL tear ended his college career. After graduating with a degree in petroleum engineering, he began working in the oil and gas industry. When he was laid off during the COVID pandemic, a former football teammate suggested he try out for the US bobsled team. Niederhofer competed full time from 2019 through 2022, training largely in Lake Placid, New York. At the time, he was single and able to make the arrangement work. Athletes on one of USA Bobsled's top teams can receive a stipend that caps at about $1,200 a month, he said, while lodging, food, and training expenses may be covered at the training center. But after he and Chloe got married and started to grow their family, the full-time professional bobsled lifestyle no longer made financial sense. Niederhofer moved his family to Midland, where he restarted his engineering career. He still hoped to return to bobsled, though, and eventually found a company willing to let him work remotely during training and competitions. That flexibility helped him resume the sport without giving up his primary income. In 2025, he finished fourth at the world championships, putting him in contention for the Olympic team the following year. A way to bring the family along The 2026 World Cup schedule created a new challenge: Every race was in Europe, culminating in the Winter Olympics in Italy. To have a shot at the Olympic team, Niederhofer would need to spend months overseas, training and competing before the January team announcement. He and Chloe decided they needed to find a way for the whole family to travel with him, rather than spending so many months apart. Renting out their Midland, Texas home helped Niederhofer's family travel with him during his Olympic season. Courtesy of Boone Niederhofer The couple had learned about Furnished Finder while looking for temporary housing in Lake Placid. As their Olympic-season plans came together, they realized they could also use the platform to list their Midland home. Before leaving, they packed up their kid's toys, moved most of their belongings into the attic, and swapped a crib for a queen-size bed. "It kind of did feel like we were moving," Niederhofer said. "And then, when we got back, it felt like we had to move back in." They received a lot of interest from prospective renters, Niederhofer said, but waited for tenants who could stay for most of their time away and minimize turnover. They ultimately found two travel nurses who rented the home from early November through the first week of March. A friend in Midland served as a local point person while the family was abroad. The rental income helped fund the family's Olympic-season travel, Niederhofer said. Business Insider reviewed a mortgage statement confirming his ownership of the home, as well as correspondence with a mid-term tenant about renting it for $2,800 a month. For him, the mid-term format offered a useful middle ground: potentially higher rent than a traditional yearlong lease, without the frequent guest turnover and cleaning that come with a short-term rental. "If you're having one turnover every three or four months, you really are only having to do something three or four times a year," he said. A 'blue-collar' Olympic sport Niederhofer learned he had made the Olympic team on January 19. The financial payoff, however, was modest. Making the team has led to some free supplements and clothing, he said, but no significant sponsorship income. Niederhofer is eligible for the Stevens Award , a new program that provides Team USA athletes with financial support later in life. The program will provide eligible athletes with $100,000, paid over four years starting 20 years after their first Games or at age 45, whichever comes later. Niederhofer competed for Team USA at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy. Courtesy of Boone Niederhofer That future benefit doesn't change the day-to-day economics of competing. "Bobsled itself is very much a blue-collar sport," Niederhofer said. "Nobody's in bobsled for the money." He and Chloe plan to continue using real estate as an additional source of income. If they travel for another competition season, they know they could rent out the home again — and if they eventually need more space and upgrade their primary residence, they plan to keep the Midland house as a long-term investment property. For now, Niederhofer is recovering from another ACL tear and preparing for a possible run at the 2030 Games. "In my whole life, all I really ever wanted to be was an athlete," he said. "The fact that I've gotten to be an athlete into my 30s has been just a dream come true." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: OpenAI pauses $200 Pro tier as Astra demand strains capacity
items.summary: OpenAI has paused new sign-ups and upgrades to its $200 ChatGPT Pro tier, citing a surge in demand for its Astra capability that is placing pressure on system capacity, according to company statements and an executive post on X. “To make sure our current users have an incredible experience and continued access to Astra, we are going to pause subscriptions to our $200 Pro plan,” OpenAI member of technical staff Thibault Sottiaux wrote in a post on X. “These put the most strain on our systems and we wanted to take the smallest step that allows us to continue giving the broadest access possible.” The company separately confirmed the move in its help documentation, stating that “as of September 10, 2026, we’re temporarily pausing new sign-ups and upgrades to the ChatGPT Pro $200 plan (Pro 20X).” The pause applies to users across Free, Go, Plus, and Pro $100 tiers seeking to upgrade, while “existing ChatGPT Pro $200 subscriptions … are not affected by this pause,” it said. Sottiaux added that “there is no impact to existing accounts and we are working on adding more capacity as fast as we can,” pointing to ongoing efforts to scale infrastructure in response to demand. Users who cancel or downgrade during the pause will not be able to re-subscribe to the $200 tier until the restriction is lifted, according to the company’s help page. The $100 Pro tier remains available, with lower usage limits. Promotions tied to the $200 tier are also paused, the page read. Astra demand drives capacity decisions The decision is directly tied to the uptake of Astra, which OpenAI has positioned as a more advanced capability within its platform. The scale of that demand, according to Sottiaux, has been atypical. “Demand for Astra is really unprecedented,” he wrote in the post. “We’re pulling all the levers possible to sustain the demand, but I’ve not seen anything like it until now and we went through very steep growth before.” He added that “priority will always be to keep excellent service for existing users,” noting that the company “might have to pause new Pro subscriptions for a bit if this continues.” The pause comes amid broader rollout challenges tied to Astra. OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman recently described the launch as “messy” after some paying users were unable to access the model immediately, reflecting the operational complexity of deploying high-demand AI systems at scale. Capacity constraints surface for enterprise workloads The pause, analysts said, reflects how demand for high-intensity AI workloads is intersecting with infrastructure limits, particularly at the highest usage tiers. “It signals that frontier capacity is still rationed,” said Bhupendra Chopra, chief revenue officer at Kanerika. “One week after launching Astra, OpenAI paused new sign-ups and upgrades to the $200 Pro tier, the plan with the heaviest Astra usage limits, while the $100 Pro tier, the API, Business and Enterprise all stayed open. That tells you the priority order.” “Consumer power users are the release valve. Enterprise contracts are what the vendor protects,” Chopra said. “For CIOs the lesson is that a model being announced and a model being available to your workloads at the volume you need are two different events.” Chopra said the move reflects how access to advanced AI capabilities is being managed. “We are already there,” he said. “Rate limits, usage caps, queueing and now sign-up pauses are all forms of capacity gating, and every frontier vendor uses some of them.” “A subscription buys you a place in the line. A fixed slice of compute comes only from a contract that says so,” he added. Planning for constrained supply For enterprise IT leaders, Chopra said model capacity should be treated as a dependency. “Treat model capacity like any other supply chain dependency,” he said. “Ask the vendor three questions before you sign. What throughput is contractually committed, what happens to my workloads when demand spikes, and how quickly can I fail over to another model.” “If a workload is production-critical, it should run on an enterprise agreement with committed capacity… and it should have a second model tested and ready,” he said. items.summary_html:
OpenAI has paused new sign-ups and upgrades to its $200 ChatGPT Pro tier, citing a surge in demand for its Astra capability that is placing pressure on system capacity, according to company statements and an executive post on X.

“To make sure our current users have an incredible experience and continued access to Astra, we are going to pause subscriptions to our $200 Pro plan,” OpenAI member of technical staff Thibault Sottiaux wrote in a post on X. “These put the most strain on our systems and we wanted to take the smallest step that allows us to continue giving the broadest access possible.”

The company separately confirmed the move in its help documentation, stating that “as of September 10, 2026, we’re temporarily pausing new sign-ups and upgrades to the ChatGPT Pro $200 plan (Pro 20X).” The pause applies to users across Free, Go, Plus, and Pro $100 tiers seeking to upgrade, while “existing ChatGPT Pro $200 subscriptions … are not affected by this pause,” it said.

Sottiaux added that “there is no impact to existing accounts and we are working on adding more capacity as fast as we can,” pointing to ongoing efforts to scale infrastructure in response to demand.

Users who cancel or downgrade during the pause will not be able to re-subscribe to the $200 tier until the restriction is lifted, according to the company’s help page. The $100 Pro tier remains available, with lower usage limits. Promotions tied to the $200 tier are also paused, the page read.

Astra demand drives capacity decisions

The decision is directly tied to the uptake of Astra, which OpenAI has positioned as a more advanced capability within its platform. The scale of that demand, according to Sottiaux, has been atypical.

“Demand for Astra is really unprecedented,” he wrote in the post. “We’re pulling all the levers possible to sustain the demand, but I’ve not seen anything like it until now and we went through very steep growth before.”

He added that “priority will always be to keep excellent service for existing users,” noting that the company “might have to pause new Pro subscriptions for a bit if this continues.”

The pause comes amid broader rollout challenges tied to Astra. OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman recently described the launch as “messy” after some paying users were unable to access the model immediately, reflecting the operational complexity of deploying high-demand AI systems at scale.

Capacity constraints surface for enterprise workloads

The pause, analysts said, reflects how demand for high-intensity AI workloads is intersecting with infrastructure limits, particularly at the highest usage tiers.

“It signals that frontier capacity is still rationed,” said Bhupendra Chopra, chief revenue officer at Kanerika. “One week after launching Astra, OpenAI paused new sign-ups and upgrades to the $200 Pro tier, the plan with the heaviest Astra usage limits, while the $100 Pro tier, the API, Business and Enterprise all stayed open. That tells you the priority order.”

“Consumer power users are the release valve. Enterprise contracts are what the vendor protects,” Chopra said. “For CIOs the lesson is that a model being announced and a model being available to your workloads at the volume you need are two different events.”

Chopra said the move reflects how access to advanced AI capabilities is being managed.

“We are already there,” he said. “Rate limits, usage caps, queueing and now sign-up pauses are all forms of capacity gating, and every frontier vendor uses some of them.”

“A subscription buys you a place in the line. A fixed slice of compute comes only from a contract that says so,” he added.

Planning for constrained supply

For enterprise IT leaders, Chopra said model capacity should be treated as a dependency.

“Treat model capacity like any other supply chain dependency,” he said. “Ask the vendor three questions before you sign. What throughput is contractually committed, what happens to my workloads when demand spikes, and how quickly can I fail over to another model.”

“If a workload is production-critical, it should run on an enterprise agreement with committed capacity… and it should have a second model tested and ready,” he said.

A recurring pattern

Chopra said the pause reflects a broader pattern seen in recent launches.

“This is at least the third time in two years OpenAI has throttled or paused access at launch,” he said. “Each launch outruns capacity, capacity catches up, and the next model outruns it again.”

“OpenAI calls this pause temporary, and it will lift once capacity catches up,” he added. “The structural condition… will persist as long as model capability keeps outpacing data center buildout.” OpenAI has not provided a timeline for when new sign-ups to the $200 Pro tier will resume, stating only that the restriction is temporary.

items.title: 'Healthcare professional' has dethroned 'influencer' as the dream career for young adults
items.summary: Alix Earle is a top influencer. Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images What do teens want to be when they grow up? Influencer or doctor? The two careers are top choices, with healthcare edging out creators by 0.2%, per a new survey. The influencer dream might be facing a reality check, though. Influencer, YouTuber, content creator . In recent years, these have been the top answers to the age-old question: "What do you want to be when you grow up?" That dream might be losing some of its luster. A recent survey of American teens and young adults found that medical and healthcare careers came out ever-so-slightly on top of becoming a creator and influencer. Clothing brand PacSun and analytics company GlobalData surveyed more than 6,000 US teens and young adults ages 11 to 24. The survey asked which careers respondents were interested in pursuing, and they could choose multiple career paths. Last year, PacSun's survey found that the influencer career was the top choice (22.2%), while medical careers came in second (19.4%). In 2026, however, influencer declined to 18.8%, slightly behind healthcare at 19%. Healthcare careers are seeing broad growth. Jobs from nurse practitioners to psychiatric technicians could witness a boom in the next decade , according to a recent job projections report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Is the influencer dream fading? Fancy trips, free things, and millions of fans — just for posting to social media? From the outside, the influencer lifestyle can seem like a dream come true. However, being an influencer is ultimately a job, whether it's a full-time gig or a side hustle. Like many jobs in the current economy, there's plenty of uncertainty surrounding it. For one, it's getting harder to make it big as a creator, as the virality jackpot grows more competitive in a saturated space. Influencers in the US are expected to earn over $21 billion from brand deals and platform revenue in 2026, according to Business Insider sister company EMARKETER. However, an influx of influencers at the lower end of the market has increased income inequality in the creator economy. Meanwhile, platforms like YouTube are making it tougher to qualify for monetization programs and cash out. Then there's the looming threat of AI. Social media, broadly, is also in the throes of a PR nightmare. Headline-making child safety and teen addiction lawsuits are shaping how a generation views the social media apps many use every day. In 2025, Pew Research Center found that about half of teens (48%) said social media has a "mostly negative effect on people their age." There's an even bigger anxiety hanging overhead for Gen Z and Gen Alpha — and that's the job market writ large . PacSun's survey showed a decline in interest across all job categories, including art, fashion, skilled trades, tech, and entrepreneurship. The one category that had an uptick: "Not sure yet." items.title: I'm a mom who switched to 'Buy Canada' 6 years ago. It takes certain sacrifices, but I wouldn't go back.
items.summary: Sarina Cornthwaite has been participating in the 'Buy Canada' movement for 6 years. Courtesy of Sarina Cornthwaite Sarina Cornthwaite is a stay-at-home mom who has been participating in 'Buy Canada' for 6 years. She said she doesn't mind buying non-Canadian products as long as it's not from the US. The biggest challenge is balancing the budget while shopping local. This as-told-to essay is based on conversations with Sarina Cornthwaite, a 35-year-old stay-at-home mom. She is based in Muskoka, Canada. Her words have been edited for length and clarity. Since the Buy Canada movement started last year, I've seen so many more of my family and friends participate and become more conscious of where their money is going. But being a stay-at-home mom, of course, I'm on a budget. Six years ago, we had just moved to a new town in Canada, and then four months later, the pandemic hit. I saw how many small businesses in our town had to close, and my husband and I started thinking, what can we do to try to support Canada through this? I've always tried to thrift and be more conscious, but buying from Canadian businesses and Canadian products became a huge priority for my family, especially when so many imports were being shut down, and we weren't sure what the full scale of things would be. We've prioritized buying Canadian ever since. Some things are more expensive to buy locally, but I've found a way to balance our budget. I budget much differently now During the pandemic, I discovered that a few grocery stores near me were selling boxes of locally grown produce for around 30 to 40 Canadian dollars. These stores were typically out of my budget , but with this deal, I was able to buy local and try new things while staying within it. My produce has become cheaper since switching to all-local, and I've subscribed my family to a weekly food box of all-local produce from Eat Local Muskoka, a neighborhood farm-to-table cooperative. We pay around CA$150 to CA$180 a month. It's fresh, I never have to wonder where it's coming from, and every week is a surprise for me, which is fun. Getting these local produce boxes helped me look toward our local butchers for meat instead of just going to the grocery stores . Some of our local butchers offer meat boxes priced between $150 and $300, depending on size. One of those boxes keeps us going for about a month, depending on how much meat we need. Our current food budget is roughly between CA$900 and CA$1,000 monthly for our family of three, up from the CA$600 to CA$700 I was paying a couple of years ago. Switching to local products definitely made me budget for things much differently. We skip eating out for the most part now, and when we do, we prioritize restaurants that feature local food. We also allocate any additional funds in our grocery budget toward sourcing more high-quality local meat and seafood. I try to buy around 95% Canadian, but there are exceptions As much as I'd like to buy brand-new Canadian products all the time, I know it's not feasible. The biggest challenge is balancing my budget with Canadian-made pantry staples, especially things like flour and beans. Sometimes I'm just not willing to pay $10 or more for a barbecue sauce made in Canada when I can get something similar made somewhere else, as long as it's not made in the States. We shop at an Asian supermarket when we can and stock up on sauces like soy sauce and bulgogi sauce. They're not made in Canada, but they're not made in the States either. For clothing, I want to make sure a brand is talking about where its warehouses are. I know the fabric might not be sourced in Canada, and that's fine, but if they're making the product here and being very transparent about that, that gives me a win for sure. I try to budget for a trip to one of our local Canadian boutiques once a year to buy one fun new piece for myself or my husband. The way I help myself stay on budget is by focusing on buying secondhand for electronics and clothing. Even though most of ours may not have been made in Canada, they were purchased through local thrift or liquidation stores, supporting our local economy that way. The Buy Canada movement has been inspiring It's been awesome to see more of my friends and family participate. A lot of my friends are other moms looking for the best deals, so we can share what we find. Some of my friends now buy a quarter or a half of a cow from Ontario farmers and stock their freezer instead of going to the butcher. Some have gone as homegrown as possible, buying their flour locally and growing as many fruits and vegetables as they can themselves. They're canning and preserving it to keep their households going. I wasn't surprised when the tariff stuff fell through last month, as it's been a disaster for a while. Seeing the Buy Canada movement get kind of reignited has been inspiring. I'm on social media a lot, and so many people are looking for Canadian recommendations. On Facebook, people are reposting Canadian alternatives to many favorite brands. I've discovered so many more new brands and companies coming out. I know the Canadian brands that are huge and well-known, but there are many smaller indie brands just starting out that are phenomenal. They're getting their moment now. Would you like to share your response to the US-Canadian tariff policy? If so, reach out to this reporter at aapplegate@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The AI doomsdayers aren't new. You just weren't paying attention.
items.summary: Tech workers have warned about an AI apocalypse for years. Why is it so viral now? Kirill Rudenko/Getty Images Jacob Coxon's resignation from Anthropic sparked a viral debate about AI extinction fears. Tech has been full of doomsdayers for years. Sam Altman said AI would probably "lead to the end of the world" in 2015. The question remains: Why do we suddenly care? Employees of the big AI labs are debating the death of the human race — again. If you've missed the apocalyptic chyrons on your TV and front-page headlines, former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon warned that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." The X post set off a firestorm of AI lab employees building their own extinction theories and spitballing percentage chances of imminent death. For many, that feels shocking. But let's be real: AI doomerism has run rampant in Silicon Valley for years. Way back in 2015, Sam Altman called superintelligence the "greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity." The sentiment continued to 2026; in May, Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark said there was a "non-zero chance of killing everyone on the planet." So, what's with the sudden interest? Maybe it's that Coxon's post puts it more plainly than the deluge of open letters and research reports, or that he was leaving Anthropic after mere months. Maybe it's fueled by recent worrying signs of AI going rogue, like the Hugging Face hack . Or maybe the post merely lit a match under an already pessimistic public. "People have been making the same exact claim for as long as I can remember," said Melanie Mitchell, a professor at the Santa Fe Institute. "I'm a bit baffled by why it's gone so viral." A history of AI worries Let's take a brisk walk down memory lane of past Business Insider headlines. In May 2023 : Business Insider In March 2024 : Business Insider And in September 2025 : Business Insider And don't forget one of Sam Altman's classic 2015 quotes : "I think that AI will probably, most likely, sort of lead to the end of the world. But in the meantime, there will be great companies created with serious machine learning." AI doomerism has been a constant drum beat in Silicon Valley's builder class — not just warning of an AI jobs wipe-out, but total annihilation of the human race. The bigger question is, why haven't we taken them seriously? For one, the message isn't always easy to empathize with. Tech employees sign open letters , and research organizations issue reports. OpenAI alum Gabriel Petersson seemed to understand this about Coxon: "He is the first relatable person to say it." The message also looks stark in comparison to the polished, professional message coming from the labs' communications teams. Meta has embraced a sunshine-and-rainbows approach to AI. Dario Amodei, while often criticized for his dire AI predictions, wrote an essay against "thinking about AI risks in a quasi-religious way." But the labs' public messaging may not match the employees' personal opinions — as the Coxon saga makes clear. While Altman warns about the "trap of doomerism," one of his employees posts about why he thinks there's a 70% chance of human extinction in the next three years. Thomas Larsen, a researcher at the AI Futures Project, said it was an "open secret" that many AI lab employees felt as Coxon did. "I feel like it was this little blip where the AI companies pushed hard towards positivity," Larsen said. "That wasn't honest." Are we ready to listen? In July, rogue OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face — and cracked open a whole new layer of AI worry. Larsen said that the hack heightened his nervousness and thought the feeling was common. People from outside the San Francisco bubble read about it; politicians like Bernie Sanders wrote about it. The incident was "one of the reasons why there's so much energy," he said. Mitchell, the professor at the Santa Fe Institute, isn't as worried; she called the fears of extinction "far-fetched." Instead of linking the Hugging Face hack itself to Coxon's virality, as Larsen did, she pointed to the stories written about it. "There's been a lot of emotional coverage in the media," she said. "I think that's fueling a lot of people's fear." AI also isn't all that popular right now — and Coxon's post may just be one more reason for a hater to hate. Larsen theorized that the public is "more receptive to the doom" simply because many don't like the tech. Hamza Chaudhry, an AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, said the public reaction to Coxon's post was the product of an "accumulation affect." AI weaponry, surveillance tools, deepfakes and job displacement are all causing worry, he said. "The reason this took off, for me, is a pressure valve," Chaudhry said. "This thing is coming, and it feels like it's coming too fast. I think those forces united behind this tweet." Read the original article on Business Insider
