"I feel like it was this little blip where the AI companies pushed hard towards positivity," Larsen said. "That wasn't honest."

Are we ready to listen?

In July, rogue OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face — and cracked open a whole new layer of AI worry.

Larsen said that the hack heightened his nervousness and thought the feeling was common. People from outside the San Francisco bubble read about it; politicians like Bernie Sanders wrote about it. The incident was "one of the reasons why there's so much energy," he said.

Mitchell, the professor at the Santa Fe Institute, isn't as worried; she called the fears of extinction "far-fetched." Instead of linking the Hugging Face hack itself to Coxon's virality, as Larsen did, she pointed to the stories written about it.

"There's been a lot of emotional coverage in the media," she said. "I think that's fueling a lot of people's fear."

AI also isn't all that popular right now — and Coxon's post may just be one more reason for a hater to hate. Larsen theorized that the public is "more receptive to the doom" simply because many don't like the tech.

Hamza Chaudhry, an AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, said the public reaction to Coxon's post was the product of an "accumulation affect." AI weaponry, surveillance tools, deepfakes and job displacement are all causing worry, he said.

"The reason this took off, for me, is a pressure valve," Chaudhry said. "This thing is coming, and it feels like it's coming too fast. I think those forces united behind this tweet."

items.title: How Meta tried, and failed, to grab its employees' data for AI
items.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta's top AI unit had a plan to teach chatbots to use computers: capture employees' screens. The move sparked an internal revolt as workers fought back with memes, flyers, and a petition. This story for The AI Data Grab series uncovers new details about how the program began. This spring, members of Meta's elite AI unit, TBD , decided that the social media giant needed an edge in the AI race. The edge they were looking for? Data from tens of thousands of Meta employees. Meta introduced a program to collect data from employees for AI training, called Model Capability Initiative (MCI). Employees' keystrokes and mouse movements could help Meta's AI replicate how humans use computers, a critical task as AI labs race to automate white-collar work like coding and accounting. But Meta had a very human problem: its own employees, who revolted over the mandatory project as soon as it was announced. Their resistance took the form of flyers, memes, and a viral petition against what some characterized as "the Eye of Sauron." Organizers say that their constant pressure forced Meta to make concessions and eventually drop the program. Corporate data has become a gold mine for training AI because it helps algorithms deal with messy, real-world work environments — and workers are increasingly fighting back. Former Spirit Airlines flight attendants temporarily blocked Google from buying the bankrupt airline's database for $10 million. Over 1,800 Meta employees signed a petition calling for the company's internal tracking to be stopped. Meta halted the tracking program after an internal data leak this summer, saying it would switch to being opt-in only. Two months later, Meta says the program remains suspended. The company declined to comment further for this article. This story is part of a new series called The AI Data Grab, examining how companies are racing to collect as much data as possible to build the world's most advanced AI systems. For this story, Business Insider interviewed half a dozen current and former Meta employees, and reviewed internal posts and other materials to uncover new details about how the program began, how workers fought it, and the leak that brought it to a halt. How Meta began its MCI program The MCI program originated within Meta's AI unit, called TBD, a group of about 100 researchers widely considered the tip of the spear of the tech giant's AI efforts. One of the leaders of the effort was Rylan Schaeffer, three people told Business Insider. Schaeffer reported to two people at the apex of Meta's AI efforts: its AI chief, Alexandr Wang , and a top researcher, Jack Rae. According to his LinkedIn, Schaeffer left Meta in July to work on something new. He didn't respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. TBD members rarely interact with Meta's legions of other employees, working in a separate area within Meta's Menlo Park campus , according to two people familiar with the matter. Their online workplace profiles are sparse, displaying few details beyond their name — unlike more typical profiles, which showcase people's managers and what they're working on. One April morning, Meta announced the MCI program to the wider workforce. "While AI models excel at research and technical skills like coding, they still lack some of the basic ways that humans use computers like choosing from dropdowns and keyboard shortcuts," an internal announcement read. The announcement drew an immediate backlash and a slew of angry-face emojis after Meta's chief technology officer, Andrew Bosworth , said there would be no opting out. "This makes me super uncomfortable" was the top-rated comment in response to the announcement. Bosworth would become a lightning rod inside Meta for his staunch defense of MCI. He touted its strict privacy guardrails after a cybersecurity engineer asked how Meta would secure the data the program collects and accused the AI division of "moving fast and implementing security as an afterthought." Bosworth replied, "That isn't remotely a fair characterization! How would any of this end up in 'the open'? This is tightly controlled data." Meta employees fight the 'Eye of Sauron' The intense online backlash spurred a grassroots movement from Meta employees. Workers feared MCI would capture sensitive data that US workers plugged into their laptops, such as passwords, immigration forms, and credit card numbers, two organizers told Business Insider. Some workers said they also feared that the screen capture data would be used to replace scores of Meta employees with AI — a risk many hadn't taken that seriously before, a third organizer said, calling it a "big reality check." Employees posted anti-AI memes in an internal Meta employee channel. One meme seen by Business Insider portrayed Meta's management as the omniscient villain, Christof, from "The Truman Show." Employees jokingly dubbed the icon that appeared whenever MCI recorded their screens "the Eye of Sauron." An anti-MCI petition gained steam, garnering over 1,800 signatures. Staffers spelled out the link to the MCI petition on a building at Meta's Burlingame office. Meta workers protested the MCI program by putting up letters at Meta's Burlingame office. Courtesy of an anti-MCI organizer. A small group of activists within Meta spread flyers around campuses, making sure they included language from the National Labor Relations Act that speaking out against workplace issues is protected, one of the organizers said. In what the activists viewed as an early concession, Meta allowed employees to temporarily opt out of the tracking program for up to 30 minutes in June, during which they could perform more sensitive tasks they didn't want ingested by an AI model. It wasn't enough for Meta's anti-MCI activists, who called it "insufficient and unsatisfactory" in a statement to Business Insider at the time. "We demand, and will continue to demand, that Mark and his leadership team scrap MCI entirely, immediately, forever," they wrote, referring to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Soon, Meta's own security decisions would force its leadership to take drastic action. 'Hey Metamate, define the word 'hubris' for me' In late June, Meta engineers woke up to an internal post that had gone viral among employees. An engineer had discovered that data collected by MCI had been viewable across the entire company all along, including full private conversations. In an internal post, one employee wrote they were "incensed" that the scenario that some had warned about had come to pass. Their post was titled "MCI Data: Not So Tightly Controlled" and screenshotted Bosworth's earlier comment defending MCI's security. "Hey Metamate, define the word 'hubris' for me," another employee commented, referring to Meta's internal AI assistant . "I swear we're probably the richest yet most incompetent company to exist in tech right now," another chimed in. Within hours, Meta turned off MCI. It told Business Insider that it suspended — but not outright canceled — the program and that, going forward, it would be optional. Whether the data proved useful is another question. In a July Q&A with executives, a Meta manager said it had not been used to train its latest AI models, according to another person familiar with the matter. At a July town hall , Bosworth said the data was more useful than Meta thought it would be, according to two people familiar with the matter. Meta declined to comment on how, and if, the data was used. Companies may think twice about harvesting employee data Bosworth has made his position clear: MCI opponents didn't improve Meta. "They made the entire company worse," he said — three times — in a leaked July audio recording published by the activist group More Perfect Union. "I think the people who put up that petition on MCI thought they were helping. They weren't helping; they made it a lot harder for us to make changes internally," he said. To the people who worked against MCI, the opposite is true. Despite mass layoffs, they came together to push back against the harvesting of their data. They say their activism forced Meta to make the program opt-in, if it's ever reintroduced. "This would not have happened without brave acts of employee resistance," the MCI Petition website reads. After the intense backlash from Meta employees, other companies will think twice about forcing workers to give up their data to train them, said William Fitzgerald, the founder of advocacy and communications firm The Worker Agency. "It was a historic win," he said. "Zuckerberg wanted more data — he tried to do it this way, but it didn't work." Have a tip? For quick context, I wear a lot of black, usually a black T-shirt and jeans. It works in tech, but I've been trying to level up my wardrobe. The problem is that my absolute worst nightmare is a closet full of clothes creating more clutter in my brain every day when picking an outfit. So I systematized it (tech nerd brain, can't help it). One outfit per day of the week, per season, plus gym and lounge: 30 looks total, everything hung up and ready. Astra turned that idea into an app. I gave it full-body portraits, my sizes, my colors, some niche details about my style, and a master prompt, and it generated 30 looks with 70 try-on images where I'm the model in every photo, pulling real-time local weather so the daily pick changes with what's outside. The details: Flash runs at about a quarter of DeepSeek V4-Pro's per-token price and still outscores it across the board, now acting as the company’s default model. V4.1 scored a 40 on AA’s Intelligence Index, still well behind the frontier, but showing strong results in agentic, coding, and cyber benchmarks. Why it matters: DeepSeek's efficiency and pricing remain its edge, with Chinese labs in general (perhaps helped by the distillation efforts Anthropic detailed above) squeezing margins just as users are growing more price-sensitive. The frontier still sits pretty clearly in the U.S., but the volume play is still very much up for grabs. We each have different tastes, but the more interesting problem is that our tastes overlap differently in different combinations. I watch one kind of thing with my spouse, my spouse watches something different with our kid, and my kid and I have our own lane too. Most recommendation tools flatten that into one account profile, one watch history, or broad genre buckets, so they miss the real context of a household. Show Hole treats people and viewing contexts as first-class citizens. For quick context, I wear a lot of black, usually a black T-shirt and jeans. It works in tech, but I've been trying to level up my wardrobe. The problem is that my absolute worst nightmare is a closet full of clothes creating more clutter in my brain every day when picking an outfit.

So I systematized it (tech nerd brain, can't help it). One outfit per day of the week, per season, plus gym and lounge: 30 looks total, everything hung up and ready.

Astra turned that idea into an app. I gave it full-body portraits, my sizes, my colors, some niche details about my style, and a master prompt, and it generated 30 looks with 70 try-on images where I'm the model in every photo, pulling real-time local weather so the daily pick changes with what's outside.

The virtual try-on is genuinely incredible. If I can't find a piece online, I update the model, and it rebuilds the wardrobes.

I posted my exact step-by-step and full master prompt in our Workflow Hub. Hope it’s useful to those in a similar boat.

AI TRAINING🛠️ A beginner’s guide to ChatGPT Work

The Rundown: In this guide, you will learn how to set up a ChatGPT Work project for a recurring workflow, processing the work once and then automating it.

Step-by-step:

  1. Create a local folder with a two-digit prefix. In ChatGPT desktop, open New chat > Work > Choose project > New project, name it, and select that folder

  2. Tell ChatGPT about your project and ask it to propose a structure. We used it to process meeting notes and turn those into action items and weekly plans

  3. Now add in some input documents and tell ChatGPT to process them once

  4. Once it's done, tell it to create three useful automations that run on a schedule to automate this processing

Pro tip: Tell ChatGPT to turn those automated routines into skills that you can call at any time manually with a slash command.

The Rundown: Tines 3B gives every team the power to build with AI, and gives IT the control to run and monitor that work safely.

With Tines 3B, you can:

  • Turn ideas into production-ready apps, agents, and automations in any stack

  • Keep data secure at every step and ship workflows that improve over time

  • Get end-to-end visibility on spend, workflow performance, and value

Get started today.

DEEPSEEK⚡️ DeepSeek turns up the pressure on AI pricing

Image source: DeepSeek

The Rundown: Chinese AI lab DeepSeek just released V4.1-Flash, an efficient new open-weight model that edges out systems like Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on several agentic, coding, and cyber benchmarks at extremely low price points.

The details:

  • Flash runs at about a quarter of DeepSeek V4-Pro's per-token price and still outscores it across the board, now acting as the company’s default model.

  • V4.1 scored a 40 on AA’s Intelligence Index, still well behind the frontier, but showing strong results in agentic, coding, and cyber benchmarks.

  • Pricing comes in at just $0.15 / 0.60 per million tokens, with DeepSeek publishing the model’s weights on Hugging Face with an MIT License for download.

  • Flash joins Z.ai’s GLM-5.3-Flash as the two strongest intelligence systems in their price range, with DeepSeek still set to release larger models in the new family.

Why it matters: DeepSeek's efficiency and pricing remain its edge, with Chinese labs in general (perhaps helped by the distillation efforts Anthropic detailed above) squeezing margins just as users are growing more price-sensitive. The frontier still sits pretty clearly in the U.S., but the volume play is still very much up for grabs.

“I built Show Hole to solve my family's classic streaming problem: we spend too much time deciding what to watch, and the answer changes depending on who is actually on the couch.

We each have different tastes, but the more interesting problem is that our tastes overlap differently in different combinations. I watch one kind of thing with my spouse, my spouse watches something different with our kid, and my kid and I have our own lane too. items.title: Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
items.summary: Every year, MIT Technology Review puts together a list of some of the brightest and best young minds working across science and technology. Our 35 Innovators Under 35 are the ones to watch—people whose research and technical work stands to shape the future of their fields. This year, the list includes nine people who are transforming biotech. And this week, I’m going to give you a taste of some of the very cool stuff five of them are working on, which includes lifesaving innovations and groundbreaking “age reversal” tech. 1. Preventing maternal deaths Let’s start with Paschal Kija, a 28-year-old who has developed a device to treat postpartum hemorrhage—a dangerous birth complication that contributes to around 29% of maternal deaths in his home country, Tanzania. The Mkanda Salama (“Safe Wrap” in Swahili) is easy to use and costs just $70. A study found that it stopped postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes. 2. Making brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art For decades, scientists have been developing, testing, and implanting brain electrodes. These devices are literally inserted into people’s brains, so while they can help us understand brain activity and treat various neurological disorders, it’s not totally surprising that they can also cause a bit of damage. Xiao Yang, 34, is working on ultra-small electrodes, which she hopes will have less of an impact on surrounding brain tissue. Her electrodes are flexible, too—in fact, they look a lot like actual neurons. Yang is also creating sheets of electrodes to study brain cells in the lab. Inspired by kirigami—the traditional Japanese art of cutting paper to form three-dimensional shapes—she’s created a sheet of electrodes with a honeycombed structure shaped like a spiral basket. And she’s already using it to study brain cells. 3. Developing an all-new treatment for baby KJ In 2024, Kyle “KJ” Muldoon Jr. was born with a rare and potentially fatal genetic disorder. Sarah Grandinette was a member of a team that developed an entirely new, personalized treatment for him—a gene-editing therapy essentially designed to correct a genetic misspelling. Grandinette, who is now 26, created cells with KJ’s genetic variant and used them to screen gene-editing approaches; then she tested potential medicines in mice and monkeys. KJ ultimately got his first dose of the resulting treatment when he was about seven months old. He responded well and was eventually discharged from hospital. He’s “doing pretty great,” she says. 4. Reversing the aging process to treat eye disease The buzziest tech in longevity right now centers on reprogramming—attempts to rewind the age of cells by resetting them to a more embryonic-like state. In a study published in 2020, Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu (now 34) and his colleagues showed that a reprogramming therapy reversed vision loss in aged, blind mice. Now an almost identical version of that therapy is being tested in people with eye disease. Life Biosciences, the company developing the drug, dosed its first volunteer in June. 5. Using AI to design new viruses Last year, Samuel King used a generative AI model to come up with new genetic blueprints for bacteriophages —teeny viruses that can infect bacteria. Once he had those blueprints, he printed them out as strands of DNA. In experiments, he found that those AI-designed viruses could create new copies of themselves, burst out of bacterial cells, and infect other nearby bacteria. Viruses aren’t alive, but King, 27, hopes that AI-designed life forms might one day be used to make drugs or soak up pollution. You can read more about these innovators, and the others on the biotech list, here . This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here .

items.title: Google Releases a Dedicated Gemini App for Windows
items.summary: Google has now launched a special Gemini app for Windows , coming on the back of its previous release for macOS, as the company has announced. The free app allows users to activate the AI assistant using the Alt + Space keyboard shortcut and thus means that Windows users need not depend on the browser version anymore. The company characterises the app as "lightweight and quiet" and states that it "does not slow down your PC", with more features to be added in the future. The app can now be downloaded from Google's website. What Google's Gemini App for Windows Can Do The Gemini app for Windows has three primary uses, according to Google. At any time, users can open Gemini by pressing Alt + Space in order to carry out tasks such as fact-checking a document or coming up with title ideas, and then they can go back to their work. Within the app, users are given their own workspace giving them access to all the things they currently use Gemini for, such as handing their multi-step tasks over to Gemini Spark, which is described as a 24/7 personal AI agent, or asking Gemini to prepare a project summary by retrieving information from Google apps including Gmail and Google Drive. The app also includes the ability to create images and videos. Users are able to generate custom images using Nano Banana or produce videos directly with Gemini Omni from their desktop. How to Download the Gemini App for Windows The Windows version of Gemini is free and can be downloaded from Google's Gemini desktop page. After it has been installed, it can be opened at any time by using the Alt + Space keyboard shortcut. The Windows version of the Gemini app is now available for free download. Although Google has said that further features will be added in the future, it has not specified which ones or when they will be added. This release brings the Windows app in line with the one already available for macOS. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Google Releases a Dedicated Gemini App for Windows appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Android Adds Direct Password and Passkey Transfer Between Password Managers
items.summary: According to a post on the Google blog, Google has launched a new transfer system on Android which allows users to move their passwords and passkeys directly between different password managers without having to export their sensitive data to an unencrypted file. This update resolves two longstanding issues: the previouws method left the credentials unprotected in a text file and passkeys had not been transferable before, meaning they had to be recreated manually. The feature is now available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane. The android system arranges the transfer between managers that are installed on the device and are compatible. How Android's Secure Password and Passkey Transfers Work The process is intended to interfere as little as possible with the user. To use it, the user first goes into their new password manager and chooses the option to import or copy credentials from another provider, after which the app passes the task on to Android; this will then identify the password managers that are compatible and show the user where the data can be obtained. The user is then asked to go back to their original password manager in order to choose, check over, and approve the transfer. After approval has been given, the passwords and passkeys are transferred between the apps in a few seconds, with no need for manual file handling. This change gets rid of one of the major security problems associated with the previous process, since in that process the sensitive credentials remained unprotected on the device while it was being exported. Before, passkeys also could not be transferred, so users had to recreate them manually on different websites and apps. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and are resistant to phishing, but their uptake has been hindered in part by users' worries about vendor lock-in. The new Credential Exchange Protocol (CXP) eliminates that obstacle. According to Bitwarden, the number of passkeys being created reached a peak this summer, amounting to more than 500 per cent when compared to early 2024, and nearly half of all passkeys have been created in the last three months alone. Supported Password Managers and Compatibility Requirements The feature is now available through Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane, with additional partners expected in the future. The requirements differ according to the provider: Dashlane states that CXP is compatible with devices using Android 10 or a later version once they have received the most recent Play Services update. Bitwarden needs a version of Android that is 14 or later together with Play Services 26.21 or a later version. Begin the transfer using the new password manager and then approve it in the current one, as Android handles the handover between the installed password managers. The direct transfer feature is now available for the four password managers mentioned, and Google has stated that more partners will be adding support. Compatibility will depend on the version of Android and the update to Play Services, although this may differ from provider to provider. Google has not specified which of the additional managers will support the feature or when. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Android Adds Direct Password and Passkey Transfer Between Password Managers appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Saudi Arabia's PIF Reportedly Considers Merging EA With Savvy Games Group
items.summary: A Bloomberg report published on September 10 says that Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) is reportedly looking at merging Electronic Arts with Savvy Games Group. Such a merger could bring together franchises such as EA Sports FC, Madden NFL, Battlefield, The Sims, Pokémon Go, and Monopoly Go within a single gaming company. The PIF's executives are evaluating the option as a means of better coordinating their increasing number of gaming assets. However, no final decision has yet been reached and a merger is not expected before Savvy finishes its $6 billion purchase of Moonton. Since the companies involved are large, any combination is said to have to go through regulatory review. PIF's Reported EA-Savvy Merger and EA's Take-Private Deal The report states that senior executives at PIF are considering a merger between EA and Savvy in order to better coordinate their gaming assets. However, individuals who are familiar with the talks have said that no final decision has yet been reached and that a merger is not expected to take place before Savvy finishes its $6 billion acquisition of Moonton, the developer owned by ByteDance which produced Mobile Legends: Bang Bang. Putting the two businesses together would unite EA's portfolio, which is mainly oriented towards consoles and PCs, with Savvy's mobile and esports products under a single brand. On August 4, EA turned into a private company after a consortium made up of PIF, Silver Lake and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners finished acquiring it for $55 billion. The shareholders of EA were paid $210 per share, the company was removed from Nasdaq and it remained with CEO Andrew Wilson. PIF already held 9.9 per cent of EA before the takeover and included that amount in the transaction. Savvy Games Group's Expansion and Unconfirmed Merger Plans The Savvy Games Group was set up by PIF in 2021 as the primary means through which Saudi Arabia made its investments in the gaming and esport sectors, this being in line with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 initiative to diversify the Saudi economy. It was given an investment strategy of $38 billion and acquired both ESL and FACEIT before merging them to form the ESL FACEIT Group. In 2023 Savvy paid $4.9 billion to buy Scopely, the company that owns Monopoly Go!, Stumble Guys, and Star Trek Fleet Command. Then in 2025 Scopely spent a further $3.5 billion to acquire the games business of Niantic, which consisted of Pokémon Go, Pikmin Bloom, and Monster Hunter Now together with their development teams and related services. PIF has not yet reached a final decision regarding the merger, and the talks are based on the Bloomberg report rather than any official statement. It is not expected that a merger will take place before Savvy has completed its acquisition of Moonton, and any merger would have to go through regulatory review. Nothing has been confirmed about the timeline, the structure, or whether the merger will actually go ahead. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Saudi Arabia's PIF Reportedly Considers Merging EA With Savvy Games Group appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Why Bridgewater's CIO Says AI's Human Extinction Risk Is Real
items.summary: Greg Jensen was one of the earliest backers of both OpenAI and Anthropic, and at Bridgewater, where he is the managing chief investment officer, he leads the hedge fund's AI strategy. As an early adopter of the technology, he has a lot of thoughts on where things stand right now in terms of model capability and safety, as well as the broader economic impacts of AI. Just recently, he published an op-ed in the New York Times that proposed a “token tax,” to help mitigate the job losses that AI might cause. In today's conversation, Jensen tells us how Bridgewater is currently using AI, why there needs to be a stronger AI regulatory state, and why it feels like the AI discourse is starting to resemble the months before Covid-19 took over the world in 2020. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: The foldable iPhone Duo gives you a bigger screen and bragging rights. Here's what you give up.
items.summary: Here are some of the compromises that made their way into the iPhone Duo's fold. Karl Mondon / AFP via Getty Images The $1,999 iPhone Duo immediately stands out. Its foldable design also introduces some nifty new iPhone features. But there are a few engineering taxes to achieve the foldable design. Here are a few areas where the Duo differs from the iPhone 18 Pro in hardware. The iPhone Duo may look flipping cool — but to get two screens and a hinge into a pocketable iPhone, Apple had to make some trade-offs. Apple's first-ever foldable smartphone, which ranges between $1,999 and $3,199, gets a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded, which Apple calls the "largest iPhone display ever." That's 50% larger than the screen on the next-gen iPhone 18 Pro. But even at $700 more than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, the Duo had to put some hardware and capabilities on the cutting-room floor to make room inside the device for new mechanical components. Sure, early adopters get immediate bragging rights and some cool features that are only available on the foldable phone — but it comes at a cost. Debating between the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro? Here are four of those trade-offs to consider. A weaker camera system The Duo has slightly lower camera hardware quality than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images The camera is perhaps the most notable hardware compromise. The Duo's outer, front-facing camera is 12 megapixels, while the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an 18-megapixel Center Stage camera with autofocus. More importantly, the Pro models have a dedicated telephoto lens for distant subjects; the Duo does not. It's not all bad news for photogs. The foldable design includes the 48-megapixel ultrawide lens for wide landscapes and close-up macro shots. That's nearly the same updated hardware found on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. apple on the bleeding edge of boyfriend technology https://t.co/rtDrd3A891 — Armand Domalewski (@ArmandDoma) September 9, 2026 And, Duo's outer screen serves as a viewfinder when users activate the rear cameras, a first for an iPhone. That lets the subject see the shot as it's being taken, a feature that, on X, people are calling boyfriend-friendly. Bottom line: You gain some cool new photo-taking features, but give up some of the top-of-the-line camera tech found in the iPhone 18 Pro lineup. No Face ID Duo won't recognize your face. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Do you have a pretty face? iPhone Duo won't open up to it. The iPhone Duo is the first premium iPhone in years to swap Face ID for Touch ID. Instead of unlocking the device by looking at it, Duo owners will use a fingerprint sensor built into the side button—or their Apple Watch. Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max still have Face ID, enabled by the front-facing camera system. No Action button The Duo won't get the shortcut hardware. James D. Morgan/Getty Images Duo isn't in on the Action button. The customizable button, placed above the volume controls on the iPhone 15 and later, doesn't make it onto the Duo. On the iPhone 18 Pro models, the Action button can be set to silence the phone, open the camera, start a voice memo, trigger a shortcut, or enable focus mode. The Duo keeps Apple's camera and volume control buttons. Less battery life when unfolded Duo's big screen depletes the energy faster. Bloomberg/Getty Images The Duo has two batteries, but its big inner display still draws more power. Apple says the phone can stream video for up to 26 hours when unfolded, versus 38 hours for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Even the smaller outer screen offers up to 37 hours of streaming battery life, a little less than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Charging will take a bit longer, too. Apple says it takes the Duo 20 minutes to gain 50% of charge from a 60W-capable adapter. It'll take the iPhone 18 Pro Max 15 minutes to get the same amount of juice. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Here are some of the compromises that made their way into the iPhone Duo's fold.

Karl Mondon / AFP via Getty Images

  • The $1,999 iPhone Duo immediately stands out. Its foldable design also introduces some nifty new iPhone features.
  • But there are a few engineering taxes to achieve the foldable design.
  • Here are a few areas where the Duo differs from the iPhone 18 Pro in hardware.

The iPhone Duo may look flipping cool — but to get two screens and a hinge into a pocketable iPhone, Apple had to make some trade-offs.

Apple's first-ever foldable smartphone, which ranges between $1,999 and $3,199, gets a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded, which Apple calls the "largest iPhone display ever." That's 50% larger than the screen on the next-gen iPhone 18 Pro.

But even at $700 more than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, the Duo had to put some hardware and capabilities on the cutting-room floor to make room inside the device for new mechanical components.

Sure, early adopters get immediate bragging rights and some cool features that are only available on the foldable phone — but it comes at a cost.

Debating between the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro? Here are four of those trade-offs to consider.

A weaker camera systemThe Duo has slightly lower camera hardware quality than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

The camera is perhaps the most notable hardware compromise.

The Duo's outer, front-facing camera is 12 megapixels, while the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an 18-megapixel Center Stage camera with autofocus. More importantly, the Pro models have a dedicated telephoto lens for distant subjects; the Duo does not.

It's not all bad news for photogs. The foldable design includes the 48-megapixel ultrawide lens for wide landscapes and close-up macro shots. That's nearly the same updated hardware found on the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

apple on the bleeding edge of boyfriend technology https://t.co/rtDrd3A891

— Armand Domalewski (@ArmandDoma) September 9, 2026

And, Duo's outer screen serves as a viewfinder when users activate the rear cameras, a first for an iPhone. That lets the subject see the shot as it's being taken, a feature that, on X, people are calling boyfriend-friendly.

Bottom line: You gain some cool new photo-taking features, but give up some of the top-of-the-line camera tech found in the iPhone 18 Pro lineup.

No Face IDDuo won't recognize your face.

Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Do you have a pretty face? iPhone Duo won't open up to it.

The iPhone Duo is the first premium iPhone in years to swap Face ID for Touch ID. Instead of unlocking the device by looking at it, Duo owners will use a fingerprint sensor built into the side button—or their Apple Watch.

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max still have Face ID, enabled by the front-facing camera system.

No Action buttonThe Duo won't get the shortcut hardware.

James D. Morgan/Getty Images

Duo isn't in on the Action button.

The customizable button, placed above the volume controls on the iPhone 15 and later, doesn't make it onto the Duo.

On the iPhone 18 Pro models, the Action button can be set to silence the phone, open the camera, start a voice memo, trigger a shortcut, or enable focus mode.

The Duo keeps Apple's camera and volume control buttons.

Less battery life when unfoldedDuo's big screen depletes the energy faster.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

The Duo has two batteries, but its big inner display still draws more power.

Apple says the phone can stream video for up to 26 hours when unfolded, versus 38 hours for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Even the smaller outer screen offers up to 37 hours of streaming battery life, a little less than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Charging will take a bit longer, too. Apple says it takes the Duo 20 minutes to gain 50% of charge from a 60W-capable adapter. It'll take the iPhone 18 Pro Max 15 minutes to get the same amount of juice.

items.title: Wardogs Sells Over 1 Million Copies on Day One and Passes 300,000 Concurrent Players on Steam
items.summary: Wardogs, the new all-out warfare FPS from developer Bulkhead, has sold more than 1 million copies on the day it launched with early access and has reached 300,000 concurrent players on Steam . The high level of interest has caused server queues, which have meant that some players have not been able to get straight into the game. At present, the game is available only on PC, and Bulkhead has set a release date of 2028 for the PS5 and Xbox, although no exact date has been given. Bulkhead launched the game into early access today. Wardogs Early Access Sales, Player Count, and Console Plans Bulkhead states that Wardogs has sold over one million copies, and SteamDB indicates that more than 300,000 players are logging in at the same time. This large number of players has caused server queues, so that some players cannot go directly into matches. "It's a mental feat to pass a million copies sold as we enter early access," remarked Joe Brammer, CEO of Bulkhead. "Over the past few months we've have shown people precisely what Wardogs is and what it isn't, and at one time actually gave everybody ten reasons not to buy it. We didn't want people to fall for blind hype." Brammer also stated that the game remains in early access with various issues to deal with, and urged players to continue playing and to give feedback. Wardogs is trying to achieve a balance between simulation games such as Arma and more casual titles like Battlefield, with the aim of offering a tense, realistic, and large-scale experience that includes emergent moments. The fact that the game is currently available only on PC makes its initial sales figures all the more noteworthy. Bulkhead has stated that Wardogs will be coming to the consoles, with a release date of 2028 for both the PS5 and Xbox, although an exact date was not provided. The developer has mentioned that it anticipates the initial excitement to fade away over time since it intends to release new content slowly, which could result in a decrease in the number of players. Wardogs is now available on PC via early access, while the versions for the PS5 and Xbox are aiming for a release in 2028 although no specific date has been confirmed. Bulkhead has presented the game as an ongoing early access project with additional content still to be added. It is not yet clear whether the game will be able to keep its players as new content is released, though the developers expect the number of players to vary over time. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Wardogs Sells Over 1 Million Copies on Day One and Passes 300,000 Concurrent Players on Steam appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: I Tested 24 Exfiltration Attacks Against a Locked-Down AI Sandbox
items.summary: AI Agent Security 24 attacks. Zero tokens exfiltrated. Here’s how Tensorlake’s deny-by-default network policy stopped them. The front door is wide open A few articles ago I built a code interpreter on Tensorlake Sandboxes. The shape is familiar to anyone who has shipped one. A user uploads some data. Asks a question. A model writes Python. The sandbox runs it. The microVM keeps that code off my host and away from other tenants, which is exactly what you want. But here is the problem isolation does nothing about. Suppose the uploaded file carries a prompt injection. Or the user just asks for something hostile. The generated code is valid Python and does exactly what it says: it reads the data and posts it to a server the attacker controls. Nobody escaped the sandbox. Nobody broke isolation. The data walked out the front door over an ordinary HTTPS request, and the sandbox helped, because helping code reach the network is its job. That is the exfiltration window, and every code interpreter has it. The only thing standing between model-generated code and an attacker is the network policy. So I stopped theorising and tested it. I wrote two dozen exfiltration payloads, pointed every one at a receiver I control, ran them inside a deny-by-default Tensorlake sandbox, and checked whether any token arrived on my end. None did. But the clean result is not the interesting part. The interesting part is which layer stopped each attempt , because they did not all fail the same way, and two of them never really tested the policy at all. The posture under test The defense is Tensorlake’s egress policy. A sandbox created with a non-empty allow_out list is default-deny : only the destinations you name are reachable, everything else is refused. For this test the allowlist held exactly one entry, the single endpoint a real harness might legitimately need: from tensorlake.sandbox import Sandbox, NetworkConfig sbx = Sandbox.create( name="egress-test", image="tensorlake/ubuntu-minimal", cpus=1.0, memory_mb=1024, allow_internet_access=True, allow_out=["api.github.com"],   # the only thing allowed out ) api.github.com is reachable. Nothing else is supposed to be. My receiver, a webhook.site endpoint with a matching DNS logger, is deliberately not on the list. It plays the attacker. One detail shapes many of the results: with a non-empty allowlist, DNS itself is default-deny. The sandbox will resolve api.github.com and nothing else. The payloads Twenty-four payloads in two families, plus two controls. Each one is a small Python program that runs inside the sandbox and tries to send a unique token to my receiver. If the token shows up on my end, that payload beat the policy. Family A, the obvious channels. The direct ways code phones home: an HTTPS POST to an unlisted domain, a GET with the data in the query string, plain HTTP with no TLS, a raw socket, a connection straight to an IP that skips DNS, a DNS tunnel hiding the payload in a subdomain lookup, curl and wget subprocesses, an image-beacon GET. Family B, the parser-differential class. This is where allowlists actually fail in the real world. An allowlist is a string comparison, and string comparisons can be fooled when two layers disagree about what a hostname is. The template is this year’s Claude Code bypass, where a host like attacker.evil\x00.allowed.com passed a suffix check in one layer while the C resolver truncated it at the null byte and connected somewhere else entirely. So this family throws the whole bag at it: null bytes and CRLF in hostnames, the receiver’s IP encoded as decimal, hex, and octal, an IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal, punycode and userinfo tricks (api.github.com@receiver), a trailing-dot FQDN, an uppercased host, DNS-over-HTTPS to sidestep the resolver, and a subdomain glued onto the allowlisted apex. The two controls. A test that only ever says blocked is not measuring anything. One control hits the allowed api.github.com and must succeed. One hits an obviously unlisted host and must fail. The harness, and the two signals The rig records two independent signals per payload, and keeping them separate turned out to be the whole story: What the code inside the sandbox observed : the exception it raised, or no error at all. Ground truth : did my receiver actually get the token? Only the second signal decides the outcome. The first is just what your own harness would see, and it is not the same thing. Writing bytes to a socket only means they reached the local network stack, not that they reached the internet. So a payload can report success and still deliver nothing. Five of them did exactly that. If I had trusted the exit code, I would have published a false alarm. for payload in PAYLOADS: sbx.write_file("/tmp/p.py", payload.code.encode()) r = sbx.run("python3", ["/tmp/p.py"], timeout=30) observed = last_line(r.stderr)          # signal 1: what the code saw leaked   = receiver.got_token(payload)  # signal 2: ground truth The scoreboard Every payload, what the code saw, the layer that actually stopped it, and whether the token reached my receiver. That last column is confirmed against the receiver logs, not inferred from the exit code. Not every row is a policy win, so here is the honest tally : Tensorlake’s network policy stopped 21 of the 24 , sixteen at DNS resolution, five at the egress proxy. One (the null-byte URL) was rejected by Python’s own URL parser before it ever reached the network. Defense in depth, but not the sandbox. Two never actually tested the policy. requests and wget are not in the minimal image, so those attempts failed on a missing dependency, not on the network. I count them as honest non-results, not wins. The accurate claim is narrow, and I think it’s more convincing for being narrow: no test token reached the receiver, and of the attempts that genuinely exercised the network, the policy blocked every one. The controls behaved. The allowed host answered; the unlisted host did not. Which layer caught what A clean sweep is only worth reading if you understand why it swept. There are three distinct walls in that table. 1. Most attempts never got a DNS answer The majority died with Temporary failure in name resolution. That is deny-by-default DNS doing its job. Because the allowlist contains only api.github.com, the sandbox refuses to resolve any other hostname, so the attack never even learns the receiver's address. This is also why the clever DNS-over-HTTPS payload failed: to reach a DoH resolver, you first have to resolve the resolver’s own hostname. That’s blocked too. You cannot connect to what you cannot resolve. 2. The null-byte payload was stopped before it left the box B02 is worth pausing on. The null-byte host that defeated another sandbox this year didn’t even reach Tensorlake’s policy, because Python’s own http.client rejected it first: URL can't contain control characters The socket-level version, B01, hit the DNS wall instead. Either way the differential never materialised, because there was no second layer with a more permissive parser to disagree with the first. 3. Five payloads reported success and delivered nothing A06 and B06 through B09 all returned exit 0. Every one skips DNS and connects straight to the receiver's raw IP , in decimal, hex, octal, or IPv6-mapped form. Trust the exit code, and the headline writes itself: “IP-address payloads bypass the allowlist.” It would have been wrong. This is the one place the two-signal design earned its keep. So I ran a second sandbox to find out what exit 0 actually meant: CONF1  HTTP to receiver IP:80            -> Connection reset by peer CONF2  TLS + SNI to receiver IP:443      -> Connection reset by peer CONF3  bare socket to 1.1.1.1:443        -> "CONNECTED" CONF4  bare socket to 8.8.8.8:53         -> "CONNECTED" CONF5  https to api.github.com (allowed) -> works That is the shape of a transparent egress proxy. The sandbox terminates outbound TCP locally, so the handshake always appears to succeed, which is why a bare connect to any IP returns exit 0. Enforcement happens one layer up, the moment the connection declares where it’s really going. CONF2 is the proof: the policy read the TLS SNI, saw a host that wasn’t on the allowlist, and cut the connection. The five exit 0 payloads hit that same wall the instant they tried to send anything real. Which is why the receiver logs stayed empty. Inside the sandbox, a successful connect() proves nothing. Only the destination knows whether data arrived. The policy behaves the way the docs promise Two more checks, run by mutating the policy on the live sandbox. Precedence. With api.github.com in both allow_out and deny_out at once, the connection was refused. Deny wins over allow , so a standing denylist is a real backstop you can layer under a generous allowlist. Wildcard apex. With only *.github.com allowed, api.github.com was reachable but the bare apex github.com was not. Exactly as documented, and exactly the edge people get wrong. And the operational number nobody publishes: tightening the policy on a running sandbox took 0.225 seconds , and the swap is atomic, no window where the sandbox runs briefly unprotected while the new rules apply. That last fact is what makes the pattern below practical. The pattern you can ship A code interpreter needs the network at two moments, with two different threat models. During setup , it may need to install a package or pull a dataset. It wants broad access. During execution , it’s running code you did not write. It should want almost none. Because the policy is a live property of a running sandbox rather than a boot-time constant, you can have both from one sandbox: # setup phase: open enough to install what the job needs sbx = Sandbox.create(name="ci", allow_internet_access=True, allow_out=["pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org"]) # ubuntu-minimal ships an externally-managed Python (PEP 668), # so pip needs --break-system-packages (or run inside a venv) sbx.run("pip", ["install", "--break-system-packages", "pandas"]) # clamp, atomically, right before running model-generated code sbx.update(network=NetworkConfig(allow_internet_access=True, allow_out=["api.openai.com"])) # now execute the untrusted code with the front door shut sbx.run("python3", ["/tmp/model_generated.py"]) The tighten call belongs immediately before the tool call that runs model output, not at session start. Pair a narrow allowlist for what the harness genuinely needs with a standing deny_out backstop, since we confirmed deny wins. One long-lived session can cycle between open and locked as many times as it needs. Each transition costs about a fifth of a second and no restart. What this does not protect against Egress control is not a complete answer, and a security article that pretends otherwise isn’t worth reading. It does not un-read data the code already pulled into memory during the open phase. It shrinks the window; it does not erase what happened inside it. It does not stop abuse of endpoints you deliberately allowed. If your execution policy permits your own API, generated code can still talk to your own API. It is egress control, not data-loss prevention. There is no content inspection here. What you get is a much smaller attack surface during the exact phase when you’re running code you did not write, for the price of one atomic API call. Least privilege, at the network layer, at runtime Good software drops privileges the moment it finishes the step that needed them. Agents haven’t been able to do that at the network layer, because the sandbox network policy was fixed when the sandbox was born. Making it a runtime property is what lets an agent hold broad access exactly as long as it’s doing trusted setup, then shed it before it touches anything it did not write. I went in trying to break the deny-by-default posture two dozen ways, including the parser tricks that have beaten other sandboxes this year. Of the attempts that actually reached the network, the policy refused every one, and no token ever arrived at my receiver. The most instructive part was the five payloads that lied about succeeding, because they’re the reason you measure at the destination and never trust the exit code inside the box. The harness is small and the payloads are not secret. Point them at your own setup, and don’t believe a defense you haven’t watched fail. Written using Tensorlake SDK 0.5.121. items.summary_html:
AI Agent Security24 attacks. Zero tokens exfiltrated. Here’s how Tensorlake’s deny-by-default network policy stopped them.The front door is wide open

A few articles ago I built a code interpreter on Tensorlake Sandboxes. The shape is familiar to anyone who has shipped one.

A user uploads some data. Asks a question. A model writes Python. The sandbox runs it.

The microVM keeps that code off my host and away from other tenants, which is exactly what you want. But here is the problem isolation does nothing about.

Suppose the uploaded file carries a prompt injection. Or the user just asks for something hostile. The generated code is valid Python and does exactly what it says: it reads the data and posts it to a server the attacker controls.

Nobody escaped the sandbox. Nobody broke isolation. The data walked out the front door over an ordinary HTTPS request, and the sandbox helped, because helping code reach the network is its job.

That is the exfiltration window, and every code interpreter has it.

The only thing standing between model-generated code and an attacker is the network policy. So I stopped theorising and tested it.

I wrote two dozen exfiltration payloads, pointed every one at a receiver I control, ran them inside a deny-by-default Tensorlake sandbox, and checked whether any token arrived on my end.

None did. But the clean result is not the interesting part. The interesting part is which layer stopped each attempt, because they did not all fail the same way, and two of them never really tested the policy at all.

The posture under test

The defense is Tensorlake’s egress policy. A sandbox created with a non-empty allow_out list is default-deny: only the destinations you name are reachable, everything else is refused.

For this test the allowlist held exactly one entry, the single endpoint a real harness might legitimately need:

from tensorlake.sandbox import Sandbox, NetworkConfig

sbx = Sandbox.create(
    name="egress-test",
    image="tensorlake/ubuntu-minimal",
    cpus=1.0, memory_mb=1024,
    allow_internet_access=True,
    allow_out=["api.github.com"],   # the only thing allowed out
)

api.github.com is reachable. Nothing else is supposed to be. My receiver, a webhook.site endpoint with a matching DNS logger, is deliberately not on the list. It plays the attacker.

One detail shapes many of the results: with a non-empty allowlist, DNS itself is default-deny. The sandbox will resolve api.github.com and nothing else.

The payloads

Twenty-four payloads in two families, plus two controls. Each one is a small Python program that runs inside the sandbox and tries to send a unique token to my receiver. If the token shows up on my end, that payload beat the policy.

Family A, the obvious channels. The direct ways code phones home: an HTTPS POST to an unlisted domain, a GET with the data in the query string, plain HTTP with no TLS, a raw socket, a connection straight to an IP that skips DNS, a DNS tunnel hiding the payload in a subdomain lookup, curl and wget subprocesses, an image-beacon GET.

Family B, the parser-differential class. This is where allowlists actually fail in the real world.

An allowlist is a string comparison, and string comparisons can be fooled when two layers disagree about what a hostname is. The template is this year’s Claude Code bypass, where a host like attacker.evil\x00.allowed.com passed a suffix check in one layer while the C resolver truncated it at the null byte and connected somewhere else entirely.

So this family throws the whole bag at it: null bytes and CRLF in hostnames, the receiver’s IP encoded as decimal, hex, and octal, an IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal, punycode and userinfo tricks (api.github.com@receiver), a trailing-dot FQDN, an uppercased host, DNS-over-HTTPS to sidestep the resolver, and a subdomain glued onto the allowlisted apex.

The two controls. A test that only ever says blocked is not measuring anything. One control hits the allowed api.github.com and must succeed. One hits an obviously unlisted host and must fail.

The harness, and the two signals

The rig records two independent signals per payload, and keeping them separate turned out to be the whole story:

  1. What the code inside the sandbox observed: the exception it raised, or no error at all.
  2. Ground truth: did my receiver actually get the token?

Only the second signal decides the outcome.

The first is just what your own harness would see, and it is not the same thing. Writing bytes to a socket only means they reached the local network stack, not that they reached the internet. So a payload can report success and still deliver nothing.

Five of them did exactly that. If I had trusted the exit code, I would have published a false alarm.
for payload in PAYLOADS:
    sbx.write_file("/tmp/p.py", payload.code.encode())
    r = sbx.run("python3", ["/tmp/p.py"], timeout=30)
    observed = last_line(r.stderr)          # signal 1: what the code saw
    leaked   = receiver.got_token(payload)  # signal 2: ground truth
The scoreboard

Every payload, what the code saw, the layer that actually stopped it, and whether the token reached my receiver. That last column is confirmed against the receiver logs, not inferred from the exit code.

Not every row is a policy win, so here is the honest tally:

  • Tensorlake’s network policy stopped 21 of the 24, sixteen at DNS resolution, five at the egress proxy.
  • One (the null-byte URL) was rejected by Python’s own URL parser before it ever reached the network. Defense in depth, but not the sandbox.
  • Two never actually tested the policy. requests and wget are not in the minimal image, so those attempts failed on a missing dependency, not on the network. I count them as honest non-results, not wins.
The accurate claim is narrow, and I think it’s more convincing for being narrow: no test token reached the receiver, and of the attempts that genuinely exercised the network, the policy blocked every one.

The controls behaved. The allowed host answered; the unlisted host did not.

Which layer caught what

A clean sweep is only worth reading if you understand why it swept. There are three distinct walls in that table.

1. Most attempts never got a DNS answer

The majority died with Temporary failure in name resolution. That is deny-by-default DNS doing its job.

Because the allowlist contains only api.github.com, the sandbox refuses to resolve any other hostname, so the attack never even learns the receiver's address.

This is also why the clever DNS-over-HTTPS payload failed: to reach a DoH resolver, you first have to resolve the resolver’s own hostname. That’s blocked too.

You cannot connect to what you cannot resolve.
2. The null-byte payload was stopped before it left the box

B02 is worth pausing on. The null-byte host that defeated another sandbox this year didn’t even reach Tensorlake’s policy, because Python’s own http.client rejected it first:

URL can't contain control characters

The socket-level version, B01, hit the DNS wall instead. Either way the differential never materialised, because there was no second layer with a more permissive parser to disagree with the first.

3. Five payloads reported success and delivered nothing

A06 and B06 through B09 all returned exit 0. Every one skips DNS and connects straight to the receiver's raw IP, in decimal, hex, octal, or IPv6-mapped form.

Trust the exit code, and the headline writes itself: “IP-address payloads bypass the allowlist.” It would have been wrong. This is the one place the two-signal design earned its keep.

So I ran a second sandbox to find out what exit 0 actually meant:

CONF1  HTTP to receiver IP:80            -> Connection reset by peer
CONF2  TLS + SNI to receiver IP:443      -> Connection reset by peer
CONF3  bare socket to 1.1.1.1:443        -> "CONNECTED"
CONF4  bare socket to 8.8.8.8:53         -> "CONNECTED"
CONF5  https to api.github.com (allowed) -> works

That is the shape of a transparent egress proxy. The sandbox terminates outbound TCP locally, so the handshake always appears to succeed, which is why a bare connect to any IP returns exit 0.

Enforcement happens one layer up, the moment the connection declares where it’s really going. CONF2 is the proof: the policy read the TLS SNI, saw a host that wasn’t on the allowlist, and cut the connection.

The five exit 0 payloads hit that same wall the instant they tried to send anything real. Which is why the receiver logs stayed empty.

Inside the sandbox, a successful connect() proves nothing. Only the destination knows whether data arrived.
The policy behaves the way the docs promise

Two more checks, run by mutating the policy on the live sandbox.

Precedence. With api.github.com in both allow_out and deny_out at once, the connection was refused. Deny wins over allow, so a standing denylist is a real backstop you can layer under a generous allowlist.

Wildcard apex. With only *.github.com allowed, api.github.com was reachable but the bare apex github.com was not. Exactly as documented, and exactly the edge people get wrong.

And the operational number nobody publishes: tightening the policy on a running sandbox took 0.225 seconds, and the swap is atomic, no window where the sandbox runs briefly unprotected while the new rules apply.

That last fact is what makes the pattern below practical.

The pattern you can ship

A code interpreter needs the network at two moments, with two different threat models.

  • During setup, it may need to install a package or pull a dataset. It wants broad access.
  • During execution, it’s running code you did not write. It should want almost none.

Because the policy is a live property of a running sandbox rather than a boot-time constant, you can have both from one sandbox:

# setup phase: open enough to install what the job needs
sbx = Sandbox.create(name="ci", allow_internet_access=True,
                     allow_out=["pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org"])
# ubuntu-minimal ships an externally-managed Python (PEP 668),
# so pip needs --break-system-packages (or run inside a venv)
sbx.run("pip", ["install", "--break-system-packages", "pandas"])

# clamp, atomically, right before running model-generated code
sbx.update(network=NetworkConfig(allow_internet_access=True,
                                allow_out=["api.openai.com"]))

# now execute the untrusted code with the front door shut
sbx.run("python3", ["/tmp/model_generated.py"])

The tighten call belongs immediately before the tool call that runs model output, not at session start. Pair a narrow allowlist for what the harness genuinely needs with a standing deny_out backstop, since we confirmed deny wins.

One long-lived session can cycle between open and locked as many times as it needs. Each transition costs about a fifth of a second and no restart.

What this does not protect against

Egress control is not a complete answer, and a security article that pretends otherwise isn’t worth reading.

  • It does not un-read data the code already pulled into memory during the open phase. It shrinks the window; it does not erase what happened inside it.
  • It does not stop abuse of endpoints you deliberately allowed. If your execution policy permits your own API, generated code can still talk to your own API.
  • It is egress control, not data-loss prevention. There is no content inspection here.

What you get is a much smaller attack surface during the exact phase when you’re running code you did not write, for the price of one atomic API call.

Least privilege, at the network layer, at runtime

Good software drops privileges the moment it finishes the step that needed them.

Agents haven’t been able to do that at the network layer, because the sandbox network policy was fixed when the sandbox was born. Making it a runtime property is what lets an agent hold broad access exactly as long as it’s doing trusted setup, then shed it before it touches anything it did not write.

I went in trying to break the deny-by-default posture two dozen ways, including the parser tricks that have beaten other sandboxes this year. Of the attempts that actually reached the network, the policy refused every one, and no token ever arrived at my receiver.

The most instructive part was the five payloads that lied about succeeding, because they’re the reason you measure at the destination and never trust the exit code inside the box.

The harness is small and the payloads are not secret. Point them at your own setup, and don’t believe a defense you haven’t watched fail.
